subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the house would give me leave to do so I should like to make a statement arising out of a number of requests made by the hon. member for Assi-niboia and others relative to the question of agriculture and what is intended to be done at the present session, as well as a general outline of that problem. I am not going into what has been done to date in connection with the development of a national agricultural program. What I intend to do is refer to one of the items in the further supplementary estimates which were tabled this morning by the Minister of Finance.
In regard to the general situation in respect of western agriculture, we made a beginning with a national agricultural program at the last session, but some of the basic problems of Canadian agriculture will yield only to long range solutions. As I see it, and I think the members of this house
will agree, the need is for a sound, comprehensive and co-ordinated program to attack specific problems and meet specific needs, but in developing a national agricultural policy we have found it necessary to deal with specific regional problems.
Our concept of a national policy is based on the belief that the national welfare demands positive action to meet the basic causes of distress and maladjustment in particular industries and regions. The agricultural policy divides itself naturally into two parts, the one being national in scope and the other being primarily concerned with specific regional problems which nevertheless form a necessary part of a national agricultural policy. In other words, regional policies must not be in conflict with but must be an integral part of the national policy.
Among the more difficult of these regional problems are those concerned with the prairie grain producers. Over the years the prairie farmer has experienced a succession of good times and bad. I have seen that situation at first hand from the time my people first went into the western provinces in 1903, and during that period of time there have been times of high income and times of low income. There have been years of almost complete crop failure and years of abundant crops. The most outstanding characteristic of the prairie farm income situation since the opening of the prairie provinces has been the variability of income. Technological improvements and marketing techniques have tended to reduce some of this variability, but as one endeavours to look into the future it would appear that this condition will remain in the western farm economy.
Averages are often used, but the use of averages in relation to farm income conceals the real problem of a large proportion of prairie farmers who are operating small farm units. While during the years 1955 and 1956, the income of the prairie farmer in general declined markedly from the level of the period from 1945 to 1952, it has been the small farmers particularly who have experienced real hardship. These farmers, whose costs of production are much higher than those on the larger farms, have lacked the necessary income to provide the essentials which have become part of an acceptable Canadian level of living.

Agriculture-Government Policy
It is therefore this problem of the small farmer, together with the general problem of the variability of farm income, which the government seeks to meet through a comprehensive farm program. During the last twelve months the government has received representations from western farm organizations with regard to deficiency payments on grain for the crop years 1955-56 and
1956-57. This problem has received the most careful consideration, in fact none which has been before us has received greater care, and a most exhaustive study has been made of all the factors involved.
The government has come to the conclusion that deficiency payments, however attractive they appear to be at first glance, would not provide a solution to the problems facing prairie agriculture but would indeed create new problems. Deficiency payments applied to deliveries of grain would fail to help those producers most in need and, if adopted, would require very large subsidies from the treasury, would inevitably lead to increased surpluses and would add further burdens in financing the disposal of those surpluses. Such payments would tend to impede essential adjustments to changing conditions of technology and demand which are essential both to the welfare of the producers and the health of the Canadian economy as a whole.
It is obvious, furthermore, that the greatest benefit from such payments would accrue to the large producer rather than to the small farmer upon whom the situation which has prevailed during the past years presses most heavily. If such payments were made on wheat alone it would constitute discrimination against the oats and barley producers, would encourage farmers to put their acreage into wheat, and would be an encouragement to additional surpluses of wheat. If such payments were made on oats and barley there is an extremely likely possibility that the United States would react in one of two ways, exclude Canadian oats and barley from their markets or place countervailing duties against them equal to the amount of the deficiency payment made. This could be particularly serious in connection with our large exports of grain to the United States, which in 1956-57 accounted for 96 per cent of our export trade in oats and 25 per cent of our barley exports.
For these general reasons we have come to the conclusion that deficiency payments to producers are not in the long run interest of either the western grain producer or the nation as a whole. It is therefore evident that the solution-not capable, of course, of achievement by a short run method-must be looked for in a long range program aimed at providing the maximum benefit to the largest

number of farmers. And of the 230,000 farm units in western Canada, approximately 63 per cent are family farm units of under 300 acres utilized for the production of grain.
Keeping in mind the needs of the majority of western farmers, the government will be submitting legislation to parliament at subsequent sessions to bring about a broad coordinated program aimed at the basic problems, namely the problem of the small farm and the problem of variability of income. This is not merely a western Canadian problem. The impact of variability in prairie farm income is felt beyond the local community. Industries which supply agriculture with production materials and equipment and those which transport, process and distribute farm products are affected as well. Serious crop failures which result in major reduction in income to western grain producers have had serious, direct and immediate repercussions on industrial activity and employment in eastern Canada. It is apparent, therefore, that a program which will bring greater stability to the income of prairie grain producers and, indeed, to farmers across the nation, is clearly in the interest of the economy as a whole.
The government therefore intends to bring into being the following far-reaching and comprehensive program designed to fill some of the gaps in our national agricultural policy which, among other things, will provide for the particular needs of western grain producers.
First, the government proposes, subject to approval by parliament at the next session, to continue the fund to assist in the export of surplus wheat stocks to non-commercial markets under the Colombo plan so as to assure the continuance of the full scale sales promotion and market development program which has been in effect during the past year. Indeed, I may say this: that one thing of which Canadians as a whole can be proud is the fact that during the past year, a difficult one for exports of wheat, Canada's exports have increased while those of other exporting countries of the world have decreased.
During the past year $50 million was taken up under this plan for assistance in securing non-commercial markets in non-commercial market areas. There are still sufficient funds available for the purpose of carrying on until the next session of parliament. In the meantime the Department of Trade and Commerce will continue without interruption an intensive program of extending markets for wheat which has been so successful during the last year.
Second, the government is studying in consultation with the provinces, and hopes as a

result of this study of this very complex and difficult problem to introduce at the next session of parliament, legislation in cooperation with the provinces which are prepared to join, to provide for a comprehensive crop insurance program. It has been one of the demands of farmers in general throughout the years that something be done to protect within reason against the uncertainties to which agriculture is subjected.
Third, in recognition of the recurring hazard of drought to the stability of livestock production in the prairie provinces, the government has taken steps to provide assistance to provincial governments, which have the prime responsibility for meeting the needs of feed deficit areas, and is giving sympathetic study to the establishment, under provincial administration but with federal financial assistance, of a forage bank program under which farmers will receive certain incentives to put up forage as a reserve against an emergency situation.
Fourth, the government is presently engaged in a comprehensive study and review of the Canadian Farm Loan Act, the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and the Veterans' Land Act, with a view to determining where enlargement of scope, expansion in function, or improvement in methods of operation may be required. Pending the establishment of improved agricultural credit facilities on a reorganized basis, the government has already taken steps to meet the demand on the part of farmers throughout Canada for increased credit through amendments to the Canadian Farm Loan Act which have increased the authorized capital of the Canadian farm loan board from $4 million to $6 million and its lending capacity from $80 million to $120 million.
Fifth, as a means of meeting the small farm problem the government has under consideration ways and means of improving the level of living for farmers on small farms by means of better land use, encouraging the formation of economic family farm units, improving technical training, extending unemployment insurance benefits to certain classes of farm workers, and by extending the vocational and technical training agreement for the benefit of those who wish to enter new occupations.
Sixth, plans are already under way for a national conservation conference, which will have important and far-reaching effects. Canadian farmers will, of course, be helped substantially through the protection given their capital resources by this national conservation program.
As I said before, the basic problems of Canadian agriculture will yield only to long range solutions. Unavoidably some time must
Agriculture-Government Policy elapse before these long range solutions can be fully implemented and their benefits made available to farmers. This proposal is an endeavour to give some temporary assistance on as equitable a basis as possible.
For a long time certain producer organizations have been advocating a two-price system for wheat, having in mind a domestic price considerably higher than the selling price of wheat for export. It is noted that the proposal applies only to wheat for human consumption. This is a proper limitation, because any attempt to impose a domestic price on wheat for feeding purposes would simply destroy the market and cause feeders to use other grains or feed products as a substitute.
There are those who feel that the establishment of a high domestic price would leave Canada in a vulnerable position if this country desires restraint on the part of other countries which subsidize wheat exports. They would argue that as long as Canada is selling wheat to domestic consumers at the same prices at which it is selling wheat abroad, no one can criticize the basis of our participation in export markets.
On the other hand, farm organizations over the years have contended that the Canadian consumer has been getting wheat too cheaply. Just as other producers expect a fair market price for their goods, so the Canadian wheat producer should receive a fair price for the wheat sold in the domestic market. That has been the general contention through the years.
Over a seven-year period the average domestic human consumption of wheat has been 45 million bushels. This is only 10 per cent of the total annual disposition of western wheat. An increase of 50 cents per bushel in the price of wheat for domestic consumption would be reflected in an increase of only 6.5 cents per bushel on the basis of total marketings. To achieve this would require a contribution to be made by parliament to the wheat board, or it would result in an estimated increase to the consumer of 2 cents per loaf of bread. Such a contribution would amount to a figure considerably lower than that which is proposed for this year only, namely the provision in the further supplementary estimates for payments to western grain producers of $1 per acre up to a maximum of 200 acres per farm in accordance with regulations of the governor in council, the amount of that distribution to be $40 million. This amount, which is designed to meet the needs of the small farmer, will be distributed by the Canadian wheat board to producers on the basis of $1 per specified acre, including acreage seeded to flax, up to a maximum of 200 acres.

Agriculture-Government Policy
A situation of emergency has developed in the western provinces which has created hardship, particularly among a large proportion of farmers whose operations are on a relatively small scale.
The long range plans now being formulated by the government will be instituted as soon as possible. They will constitute a truly national program. Several of these measures are designed to meet the particular regional problems of western farmers. The others are truly national in application and will be a potential source of help to every farmer in Canada, as has been the legislation so far introduced in connection with the Agricultural Stabilization Act. What we are trying to do is establish a concept of national policy designed to ensure equality of opportunity for all Canadians.
Continuing efforts will be made to maintain the primary industry of agriculture, and I can say that at all times we are prepared to consider proposals which will add to the completeness and effectiveness of the program, at all times, too, considering the national interest.
The immediate and long-term approach to the basic problem facing Canadian farmers is a recognition of the fact that the prosperity of Canada is indivisible and that a reasonably high and stable level of income in Canadian agriculture adds to the welfare of all Canadians. The variability of farm income in all parts of Canada-and I speak now particularly, in view of this provision in the supplementary estimates, of western Canada-affects industries which supply agriculture with production materials and equipment and those which transport, process and distribute farm products. Serious crop failures result in major reductions in income to western grain producers and in turn result in serious direct and immediate repercussions in industrial activities and employment in eastern Canada and in other parts of Canada. It is apparent that a program which will bring a greater stability to the income of prairie grain producers, and indeed of farmers across the nation, is in the interests of the Canadian economy as a whole.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has made a very important and comprehensive statement on a very important aspect of our economy, and it is not easy to deal at this time with all the points he raised. He has announced today certain short range action that is to assist grain producers in the west, and he has also indicated some long range policies that the government proposes to follow to assist agriculture.

So far as the first announcement is concerned, we recognize that there has been a growing gap between what the grain producer receives for his produce and what he has to pay for the instruments of production. We are quite sure, on this side, that the grain producers, with that problem before them, will welcome this particular assistance, will welcome this particular grant though they may be disappointed in the amount. I have no doubt that when my hon. friend from Assiniboia gets up immediately after I conclude he will call it peanuts.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: I did that a couple of days ago. I shall call it a pittance today.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Perhaps he may even refer to it as salted peanuts. However, though this may be disappointing to the grain producers, I think it has one provision that is to be welcomed; that the amount of $1 per acre shall be paid on a maximum of 200 acres, so that the very large grain growers will not benefit disproportionately to the smaller farmers.
This problem of our western grain producers is a regional problem, but it is also a problem of national importance. It seems to me that it has to be solved in a way which will keep the balance among all primary producers in this country. Otherwise the solution will not be permanent and will not redound to the national advantage as it should. While I have said that the grain producers will welcome this grant, though they may consider it too small, and it will help them up to a point to meet their special problems, there are other primary producers in this country who will undoubtedly relate this kind of assistance to their own difficulties. I am thinking particularly at this moment of the fisherman who has also had his hard times, and who perhaps will look with a certain amount of envy to this kind of action taken by the government for the grain producers.
All this means is that any action of this kind, desirable and worthy though it may be, which assists one segment of our producers, has to be kept in equitable balance with the other elements of primary production in this country or there will not be the good results that should follow from it. This means, surely, that assistance of this kind to primary producers of one type or another, to be effective and to have long range value, should be based on sound principles which can be applied to other primary producers.
This particular action, because it is a grant and is not based on any such principle-it is not based on the principle of parity prices or on any formula of deficiency payments; indeed, if I understood the Prime Minister

aright he has rejected the deficiency payment formula as the solution to the problem of our grain producers in the west-does not meet that test.
I agree with the Prime Minister when he pointed out that in the adoption and application of any formula of this kind to assist primary producers one has to be particularly careful to meet two requirements; one, not to take action which will result in a burdensome surplus which, in the long run, may hurt the producer as much as the immediate aid may help him; and second, not to take the kind of action-the Prime Minister referred to oats where such a high percentage of our crop goes to the United States, and he was using a good illustration-the kind of governmental assistance which may result in retaliation in the market to which we export our products.
I agree, therefore, that any kind of principle that may be adopted has to keep these two things in mind, but I do reiterate that there should be some principle behind assistance of this kind. Nevertheless, in so far as this action will assist, for the time being, the grain producers of the west to meet their special problems, we welcome it.
Then the Prime Minister went on to talk about some long range policies for agriculture which his government has in mind. He spoke with some satisfaction over the position in regard to wheat exports and what is going to be done to maintain and perhaps improve that position in the years ahead. It is quite true, and I think all Canadians must get a great deal of satisfaction from it, that our wheat exports have held up remarkably well this year, and in fact have increased in volume. It is true also that one reason for that increase is the export to these noncommercial markets about which the Prime Minister spoke, particularly under the Colombo plan. We welcome his statement that that policy is to be continued with increasing effectiveness, we hope, next year, so that even more wheat may be exported for that particular purpose.
But while that is true, and while good results may have been achieved in this regard this year and our wheat exports may have been increased, it must be remembered that this was due in part to this increase in the exports to non-commercial markets. It was due also to the fact that some other countries which normally export wheat had small crops. Perhaps also it is something to be kept in mind that the United States, in spite of all the devices which have been adopted to push wheat into world markets, such as barter, sales for local currency, gifts, and long term easy credit, was not able to increase its wheat
Agriculture-Government Policy sales in the last year. Perhaps there is a moral to be drawn from that which we could use in this country. It would be this, that the greater the steps taken to force wheat on the world markets in terms which are other than commercial, the more difficult it will be to sell your wheat on commercial terms. That is something which has to be kept in mind in our wheat export policy.
The Prime Minister mentioned also that consideration is being given to a system of national crop insurance in co-operation with the provinces. We shall follow these developments with great interest, because nothing could be of greater importance to agriculture than to be protected in the way he has suggested. He mentioned also the importance of agricultural credit. We on this side have for some time been advocating the consolidation and unification of all the agricultural credit facilities of the government. I know that consideration is being given to this by the government, and we shall hope there will be some results from that consideration at the next session.
Not only will it be desirable to have this kind of consolidation of agricultural credit in the interests of the farmer himself, but even more important may be the establishment of an agricultural export bank or even an export bank not limited to agriculture, to help in the way that has been done in the United States. I would say that this development of agricultural credit which the Prime Minister has mentioned has a very direct connection also with the importance of land use. The two should be tied together in this connection. Perhaps it is not inappropriate to mention that the former government set up a committee of the Senate to study this question of land use, from which good results may follow.
Today we have been confronted with an announcement by the government of short range action and a policy of long range importance. Speaking for our party, we hope the long range policy will enable agriculture to obtain its fair share of the national income, because without that there can be no prosperity in this country. We hope the long range policy will be more effective in accomplishing those objectives than the short range action to assist the grain producers at this time.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the very long statement that has been made by the Prime Minister. When a statement is made on motions, the length of the statement seems to be in inverse ratio to the acceptability of the announcement. If it is an excellent announcement it can be dealt with very quickly. If it is an announcement which

Agriculture-Government Policy is likely to be met with a good deal of criticism, then of course it is a long statement and one has to drag in a good many other things in an attempt to muddy the statement and so confuse the people who are being affected.
This statement is not new, Mr. Speaker. This $1 an acre is not new. This is another famous repetition, as we have seen so many times this session, of the press getting a very important leak from the cabinet. Whether it is a leak that is reported as a newspaper story or whether it is a document or some other matter, the press seem to be most efficient at getting advance information. Hence, with advance information in this instant having been given to the country, we are by this time able to get at least an indication of the reaction of the producers who are mainly affected, I have in my hand the Winnipeg Free Press of Thursday, August 28.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Hon. members may keep on laughing if they like. It has a story by Peter Thomson on the front page and it is quoting James Patterson, the president of the interprovincial farm union council. Mr. Patterson has referred to the $1 per acre and the $200 maximum as "a pittance". He says it will not in any way meet the needs of the prairie producers. He also says:
We certainly expected something reasonable . . . and the $25 million-
Now it is $40 million.
-falls far short ... It takes a long time to pay bills with nickels.
I could go on to other parts of the article such as this:
It will give the farmer a little "spending money" said Mr. Patterson, and the government apparently thinks that will settle matters for a while.
The farm organizations across this nation have taken the position that agricultural producers, when they are efficient, should obtain a standard of living comparable to that of other people in similiar or comparable occupations. Hence farmers over the years have asked for parity prices, prices that will give the producers a fair share of the national income. Until recent months they had believed that this government believed in parity prices. They had the statements by the Prime Minister on many occasions when he was in the opposition. They had on record of the Canadian House of Commons motions by the Prime Minister asking for parity prices. But when the Prime Minister was in a position to bring about parity prices, parity prices were dropped. Then deficiency payments became the accepted policy. We have the Agricultural Stabilization Act, and

certainly a paramount feature of that act, and a continuing feature, has been the making of deficiency payments. Only this week the Minister of Agriculture, in an announcement that we all welcomed, suggested that deficiency payments would be provided to the peach industry on a certain formula. But in this announcement the government's position is one of opposition to deficiency payments. Instead of deficiency payments we have a payment of $1 per acre up to $200. A $200 payment, Mr. Speaker, while of some value- the value of $200-will go no real distance in allowing the farmer to pay his bills, to provide his family with a reasonable standard of living and to replace his equipment when it wears out.
The farm organizations on the prairies have taken the stand that deficiency payments should be made. The farm organizations are united in that policy; and not only are the farm organizations united on it but organizations representing people generally on the prairies are in full support of this idea. The Saskatchewan wheat pool has perhaps spearheaded the drive, with full support from other farm organizations and all major organizations on the prairies. They have asked for a payment on wheat of 22 cents at least for 1955-56 and 36 cents for 1956-57, with comparable payments of 14 and 15 cents on oats and 14 and 22 cents on barley.
These deficiency payments which the farmers' organizations have requested have been worked out in an exact manner with a definite formula. They have taken the crop years from August 1, 1947 to July 31, 1955. They have averaged out the payments the farmers have received in that time, and they have said that the payments that are now made on wheat, oats and barley should be brought up to that level, that is deficiency payments of that amount. They point out that since 1947 the farmer's cost of production has gone up by 50 per cent but the price of wheat has dropped by 21 per cent. They are not asking that their position be maintained by restoring the position they had in 1947. They are not asking for a deficiency payment which would be based on the cost of production or a parity price. However, they are asking that in the years ahead they shall not receive, even with the cost having gone up a large amount, less than the average price they received in that eight-year period.
These farm organizations are very serious in this request. I do not think the $200 per farm, which amounts in total to something less than 10 per cent of the total amount of deficiency payments the farmers have asked for these two years, will in any way satisfy

these organizations or will in any way reduce their efforts to obtain a square deal for their members.
A great deal of sympathy is being expressed for the small farmer. Hence the payments, they say, are being kept to a maximum of $200 on 200 acres. I think we should be helping the average farmer including the small farmer. The average farm in Saskatchewan today is of about 500 cultivated acres.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: No.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: The Minister of Agriculture can make his speech also. It is about 500 cultivated acres.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: That is absolutely wrong.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: I am talking about the mean average.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: That is absolutely wrong.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
The Minister of Agriculture has been wrong so many times that I do not mind his being wrong again. Mr. Speaker, the average is very much higher than the 200 acres that is being set as this small limit. In asking for deficiency payments the farm organizations have not said the government should pay large sums of money to large farms. They have said there should be a maximum. They have said that the maximum should be not $200 but $1,500, and that it should be paid on a bushel basis.
I was also disappointed in the stand taken by the Leader of the Opposition. He did not come out four-square for deficiency payments. He did not come out against them, either. He took a diplomatic position, leaning first to one side and then to the other side. He wanted to be sure, along with the Prime Minister, that any action taken would not result in burdensome surpluses. All I can say to both those hon. gentlemen is that if they think the kind of payments which have been requested by farm organizations would increase burdensome surpluses, they are mistaken. The acreage which would be seeded to those grains in the prairies is a stable acreage; it changes very little. The farmer's pattern of seeding has not changed appreciably over the years. The present Minister of Trade and Commerce and other ministers of trade and commerce have pointed out so many times that it was not a huge expansion of Canadian wheat acreage which had brought about our surpluses, and so deficiency payments of the order asked for by farm organizations will not add to our burdensome surpluses because the acreage which is now being seeded to grains will in general continue to be seeded to those grains in the future.
The Prime Minister has intimated that the government has some other aspects of this
Agriculture-Government Policy farm program in view; he has talked about a surplus disposal program. We in the C.C.F. have asked for a surplus disposal program for many, many years, and when Washington was being roundly condemned for its so-called giveaways, we said it might be a better use of Canada's energy if it were spent at least in part in developing our own surplus disposal program.
As far as crop insurance is concerned, I have studied this question rather thoroughly over the years, and it is a difficult question. There are many problems connected with crop insurance; and if we are going to make crop insurance actuarially sound on an individual farm basis, as they have endeavoured to do in the United States, it means that the premium which an individual farmer must pay in the high risk areas becomes so great that it is almost impossible for him to meet his payments. Therefore any system of crop insurance cannot be the type of insurance about which we ordinarily speak, but must be a type of crop failure protection or crop failure assistance which will be supported by governments before it can be successful.
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been amended from time to time in this house. I think it is a good act and that it should be expanded. I would like to see the maximum payment, as I have said already during this session, increased to $10 per acre in keeping with today's costs of production and the other payments in the schedule set at varying amounts in accordance with that maximum. If this were done, along with increased contributions from the producers themselves and increased contributions from the treasury, we would have the type of crop failure protection which would give real financial protection to the farmer when his crop failed, and would not have attached to it the great many difficulties which ordinarily go with crop insurance.
The announcement that farmers will now be paid up to a maximum of $200, which means that most farmers will receive $200, in no way removes the necessity to keep on working for deficiency payments, to keep on working for payments based on a formula and to keep on working for a permanent policy, and not to be in any way satisfied with what amounts to a one shot affair, the $40 million put into the supplementary estimates for this year. This is not a permanent policy, this $40 million item in the estimates. We would naturally welcome any continuation of this as a permanent policy, but it seems most inadequate to keep the producers in a state of suspense by saying, "We will give you $40 million this year as a supplementary item and we will leave these other things over to a later date".

Agriculture-Government Policy
The Leader of the Opposition has said there should be a comprehensive policy for all sections of the country; he has also said that the fishermen may look somewhat critically-I do not want to misinterpret him- at this legislation, or may look at it with some envy. I have every sympathy for the fishermen as primary producers and I would certainly support, as would the C.C.F. group, any and every measure to help the fishermen of this country; but I hope we will not hear in this house members who represent ridings in which fishing is very important opposing this legislation because it does not give anything for the fishermen.
I realize, as do other members, that the fishermen today can obtain unemployment insurance under certain circumstances, while the grain producer cannot do so. The fishermen can obtain loans through their cooperatives under the fishermen's loan act, while Canadian grain producers are not able to obtain loans from co-operatives under the farm loan legislation. There is certain beneficial legislation which the fishermen now have which the grain producers do not have. We do not object to that; we are merely anxious that the benefits which today apply to fishermen may be obtained by grain producers and indeed by all producers. That is the position we take.
This $40 million will mean $200 in assistance to each qualifying producer, but in all seriousness I feel the amount is most inadequate, and that it is not a fulfilment of the statement by the Prime Minister that sympathetic consideration would be given to deficiency payments, or the statement by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources that the government was going to provide a revolutionary farm program which would include deficiency payments on western grain.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if you would inform the new hon. members of the house
under what rule of privilege the hon. member for Assiniboia is allowed to rise and speak on the first order of business. I have looked through the books and can find nothing which says that anyone other than the Leader of the Opposition should rise. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This is an item which I feel I cannot allow to pass without making a short statement. I shall not hold up the committee, but I feel that in view of the attitude taken on this side of the house and the position of the minister, which I understand, there should be at least a brief statement on it.
In the first place, as the house knows, this is an item to pay the deficit on the operation of Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships for that portion of the year during which they were in operation. It has to do also with the decision, approved by the Canadian government, to sell these eight vessels.
I should like to say here that I think that decision was a mistake. I say this having regard to what happened in the past. I think it was a mistake to have attempted in the earlier session to transfer the flag to Trinidad, and now it is an equal mistake to transfer it to Cuba. After all, what is being done is this. It is a United States company operating out of Detroit under a Cuban flag that will now operate these ships, thereby

depriving the officers and men of these eight ships, of their livelihood, apart from all of the business which was generated between the Caribbean countries and our own Canadian shore.
I think it was a mistake also because the former government had decided to effect a five-year plan under which these eight ships would have been put into operation for a period of five years to determine whether, at the end of that period, it would be advisable to wind up the operations of Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships. I realize that even then it was a marginal operation. It is for this reason I have no hesitation in saying now that that decision to transfer the flag was wrong, that the decision should not have been made, that the decision should not have been approved by the Canadian government.
Having said that, I come to the other question which is perhaps of greater importance and greater concern to the house, that is the question of a Canadian deep sea fleet. I know the position in which any minister of transport finds himself with reference to that matter. There is no doubt that following the war years it was possible to operate a deep sea fleet at a profit because the Canadian bottoms were available and bottoms from other countries were in short supply at the time. Then came the Korean war and again there was a great demand for ships and shipping services by all countries, and the Canadian deep sea fleet did operate profitably. For a period of two or three years, I believe, following that time there was an item of $3 million or $3.5 million put in the estimates of the Department of Transport in order to assist this fleet.
I know that, having regard to general policy, it is perhaps difficult for one department to bring its point of view to bear upon the whole government. I know the Canadian maritime commission and the departmental transport officials, as well as the minister, must of necessity be sympathetic to a case such as this, but the point I want to make and the blame, if any, I want to direct at the minister in as gentle a way as I can is with regard to the decision taken by the Canadian maritime commission quite some time ago that at no time should the Canadian merchant fleet ever get below 750,000 deadweight tons. This was considered by the Canadian maritime commission as a bare nucleus for a Canadian fleet and that is what we, when we were in office, were determined to maintain. We did that during all the years we were in office.

Now by the sale of the eight Canadian National (West Indies) ships, and other transfers that have taken place, this minimum requirement recommended by the Canadian maritime commission, an agency of the Minister of Transport, has been reduced away below the 750,000 deadweight tons. What it is at the moment I do not know, but I heard the hon. member for Assiniboia say yesterday, I think, that it was somewhere in the neighbourhood of 185,000 tons; of that I am not sure. My attention is directed to the fact that it is now 186,000 tons.
The point is that it is now very far below what was required as a nucleus. The question I bring to the minister's attention and ask him is this. In view of the recommendation of his own agency that the Canadian mercantile fleet should never at any time be below the figure of 750,000 deadweight tons, what does the government propose to do in the face of the recommendation of its own agency?
Before I resume my seat I feel that I should say something in answer to a criticism made by the hon. member for Danforth yesterday concerning the president of the Canadian National Railways. I had already spoken at the time; otherwise I would have risen then to say this. I did not always agree with the recommendations made by the president of the Canadian National Railways, but I always considered that he was a public servant of the highest character. I have come into contact with him over a period of nine years, and I not only respected him for his loyalty to the government which he served-and I am sure he is giving the same loyalty to the present administration-but was impressed by his full understanding of all the questions that we discussed together.
I regretted very much the reflection made yesterday upon the quality of his services. I was again brought into contact with him in my capacity as president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, and we had some bitter discussions about a matter which I know has come to the attention of the Minister of Transport. But notwithstanding those discussions I believe that he is one of the finest types of officials that the government of Canada has. I deeply regret that any member of the house should have felt it necessary to attack him under the circumstances.

To what the hon. member for Laurier has just said about Mr. Donald Gordon, president of the Canadian National Railways, I should just like to add this. I have always found, as he did while he was a member of the government, the most complete co-operation from Mr. Donald Gordon in all my dealings with him. I have complete confidence in him as president of the railways,
Supply-Transport
and I believe his energies are at all times directed to the efficient and effective operation of the railway. I believe he is doing his utmost to run that railway in an effective and efficient manner, and I have complete confidence in him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall vote 443 carry?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister did not answer my question.

In reply to what the hon. member for Laurier said earlier with regard to shipping policy generally, I should like to point out that on June 30, 1957, which after all was only nine days after we assumed office, there were only 26 ships listed on Canadian registry, 18 of which were dry cargo ships and 8 were tankers. I am now talking about deep sea ships. They had a total gross registered tonnage of 186,163. I should like to give the comparative figures for the year 1948. At that time there was a total of 172 deep sea ships on Canadian registry. Of those, 157 were dry cargo ships and 15 were tankers, and they had a total gross tonnage of 1,178,791. I think the hon. member will therefore agree that a great deal of reduction in the Canadian fleet took place under the late government of which he was a member. I just mention that matter in order to point out the fact that this reduction is something that has been going on for a long time, and that a great deal of it went on under the former government.
This matter is of concern to me and to this government. Later on this fall I intend to bring the subject again to the attention of the government, and it will be thoroughly discussed.

As has already been said by both hon. members who have spoken, Canada's merchant fleet has been reduced very rapidly in recent years. My purpose in rising was really to ask the minister whether, in view of the great interest in the transaction -I refer to the sale of the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships vessels-it will be referred next session to the standing committee of this house dealing with railways, air lines and shipping owned by the government.
I have found that a great many Canadians are not only disturbed by the fact that the Canadian merchant fleet is being very rapidly reduced, but are particularly concerned about the events surrounding the sale of the Canadian National (West Indies) steamships. There is the whole question of whether Canada received value for the ships. There is the question-and the minister has already referred briefly to this matter in the house-of other offers being made and in one instance, though the minister says the offer came late, an

Supply-Transport
offer that was higher than the sale price obtained for the ships. In the public interest -and it may be the intention of the government to do it anyway-I think this extremely important sale should be referred to a standing committee of this house so that members may inquire as to the circumstances surrounding the sale and find whether or not there is any foundation for the fears expressed by some that the Canadian government did not get for the ships the value it might have obtained.
I know the minister will say that was the very best offer the government could get. That being the case I can see no reason why, from the government's standpoint, there should be any objection to this course being followed. I think such an airing should be given to this sale.

The government has no objection at all to any members of the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping, which will of course meet next year, asking Mr. Donald Gordon any questions they wish to ask about this matter. I feel sure that Mr. Gordon will be pleased to answer fully any questions that are put to him. Neither the government nor the Canadian National Railways have anything to hide in this matter. It was a perfectly open transaction. It was a good transaction. As hon. members know, both the Canadian National Railways and the government were reluctant to sell this fleet. We took the step as the only one we felt to be sensible in all the circumstances.
As to the circumstances of the sale, the prices offered and the actual price that was accepted, there is nothing to hide with regard to any of those matters. I am sure that next year Mr. Gordon will welcome any questions about the transaction which any member of the committee would like to ask him next year.

I appreciate the answer of the minister. I myself am not certain, because I have never had the privilege of being a member of this committee, whether or not persons in addition to Donald Gordon should be called, but I take it from the general purport of the minister's answer that he is quite prepared to have a full inquiry into this transaction next year, and certainly his statement is satisfactory to me.

As far as I am concerned I am perfectly willing, but this is a matter for the committee itself to decide. If the committee decides to call somebody before it for examination, that is perfectly satisfactory to me.

With respect to this particular item, is that exactly the position of

the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamship Company? My impression has been that it is really a government operation, and it is simply put under the administration of the Canadian National Railways. So the responsibility of the government in respect of matters of policy, I think, is quite different from what it would be if we were dealing with a property which strictly belonged to the Canadian National Railways. This is simply under their administration, something like the Hudson Bay railway, is it not? I must say that I share the view of the member for Laurier in that we are very disappointed that there has not been a greater effort to carry out that five-year program.
Second, when the decision was made to sell these ships I had very grave doubts that, considering the difference between the lowest and the next lowest tender, the best decision was made in the national interest. I believe the minister, when he made the announcement about the sale, indicated that he had received some assurances from the purchaser that the ships would continue to be engaged in carrying traffic between Canada and the West Indies, which is of so much value to our national economy.
The minister is probably aware of the fact that there was an article just a week or so ago in the New York Times to the effect that this was not the intention of the purchaser over the long pull, but that just as soon as the seaway was open it was the company's intention to withdraw these ships from the West Indies trade and that they would simply be used to the best commercial advantage. That would probably be in seaway traffic and not necessarily, as it has been in the past, contributing a very important aid to Canada, largely in respect of the maritime economy, in the development of our trade with the West Indies.

Mr. Chairman, the information we have is that when the seaway is open, in addition to using the ports of Halifax and Montreal this company is considering the possible further extension of its operations to the great lakes ports, but not the elimination of the ports of Montreal or Halifax.

I am more concerned
about the elimination of the regular traffic, with the West Indies being the other end of the route. What assurance has the minister received from the purchaser in that respect?

The Canadian National (West Indies) Steamship Company was assured by the purchaser that it intended to serve the ports I mentioned when I made the announcement to this house. If the purchasing company wishes to change its mind at any time, it owns the ships and it can do so; but we

were given that assurance, which I passed on to the house and, as I have said, the only change of which we know is that it is contemplating the possibility of extending its operations into the great lakes after the seaway is open.
Would all the crews be Cuban citizens?
That, Mr. Chairman, is the business of the purchasing company. That company now owns the ships and can hire whatever crews it wishes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Under the Cuban flag they could not have other than Cuban crews, could they?
I am not too familiar with the regulations governing registry under the Cuban flag, but I would assume they would be Cubans.
Was the government or the minister given any written assurance in this matter?

I understand the purchasing company wrote a letter to Canadian National Railways to that effect but, as I say, once the transaction was completed the ships are the property of the company and it can change its plans as it sees fit.

Air Services-

449. Air services administration, $1,116,241.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This is a pretty important item in that it covers a rather wide field, and perhaps it might be advisable to call it one o'clock. If not I shall proceed with the remarks I have to make.
No; I think it would be perfectly satisfactory to do so. I agree that this would be a good place to stop.
