AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when we adjourned at one o'clock we had reached the item Air Services Administration and on this item I just want to bring one matter to the attention of the minister, and I do not want to deal with it at any length.
Supply-Transport
I did have the opportunity when the committee on railways and shipping was established to say something about air competition, and what I have to say at this moment on the subject will be brief. This is, as the committee knows, and as the minister in particular knows, a subject of extreme interest and importance, namely competition in trans-continental air routes. In view of the statements which were made earlier by the minister and others-sweeping statements to the effect that there would be all-out competition in this field-I want to tell the minister that I think he was well advised to seek advice from a British consultant and to have tabled in the house some time ago what is known as the Wheat-croft report. The Wheatcroft report clearly establishes the principle of festina lente- make haste slowly-and I believe the minister has come to the conclusion now that there should be no ill considered action taken.
As the committee knows, C.P.A. and Pacific Western Airlines have made application before the air transport board, and the matter being sub judice. I have no intention of discussing it other than to say, arising out of the Wheatcroft report, that there are three alternatives which could now apply: first, the status quo, leaving the position remain as it is; next, all-out competition; and, thirdly, a policy which would be midway between the two. That may be what the Wheatcroft report has in mind in effect- gradual competition in the field of these trans-continental air routes.
However, there are many things which come into play in deciding whether or not competition is advisable. There is the density of the traffic, there is the financial implication involved and there are, in addition, such questions as the adequacy of the service, the frequency of the service and the quality of the service. But there is one point on which the Wheatcroft report lays great stress and that is that there are only three routes in Canada where there is enough traffic to sustain competition, and those routes are Toronto-Montreal, Vancouver-Victoria and Toronto-Winnipeg.
I did attempt to discuss this matter at the committee on railways and shipping but I was ruled out of order. I think the ruling was mistaken and erroneous, particularly in view of the fact that the Wheatcroft report had been tabled in the house, but nonetheless I will not take advantage of the opportunity to discuss the matter here other than to say that I believe the effect of competition on Trans-Canada Air Lines is one thing that should be carefully considered and carefully

Supply-Transport
studied having regard not only to the Wheat-croft report but to the whole position of air traffic in Canada.
There is no doubt in my mind that there is no better air line in the world than T.C.A. I have had the opportunity in the position which the minister now holds of using many air lines but I have never found one which better deserves, in the over-all acceptance of the term, the statement that there is no finer air line in the world than Trans-Canada Air Lines. There may be certain misgivings about T.C.A.-I have no doubt there are- and some mistakes have been made, but on the whole few air lines do compare with it.
Now I wish to make a statement which I hope the committee will accept in the right spirit. It is that when men go out of public life it seems they are so often forgotten and that never again is a word said about them. I wish to refer now, in particular, to the work done with regard to T.C.A. by the Right Hon. C. D. Howe. I think the establishment of T.C.A. is a monument which will always live to his credit. I can remember many debates in this house-many heated and bitter debates-having to do with T.C.A., but I will not go into them now in order to keep away from anything which might be contentious. However, I do want to say that now that this great public servant has gone out of public life the committee should be reminded that one of the many lasting things which he accomplished for this country of ours was the establishment of one of the finest air lines in the world-Trans-Canada Air Lines.

I should like to say at this moment that I agree completely with what the hon. member for Laurier has said about Trans-Canada Air Lines and the services which it provides. I agree with him completely in that. I think it is absolutely first class, and I am very proud to be the minister who reports to parliament for T.C.A. 1 should also like to agree with him regarding the great contribution which Mr. Howe made to the building up of this fine corporation.

I want to take advantage of the opportunity afforded by this item to say that we in the C.C.F. are proud of the operations of the T.C.A. We feel that it is an outstanding example of efficiency and quality of operation. It is a tribute to and an example of what can be done by public ownership in this important field. We know the statements that have been made by government members in the past regarding Trans-Canada Air Lines have not always been complimentary. There seems to have been a great desire on the part of Conservative members to introduce an element

of so-called competition but aimed in a direction which we would suggest would reduce the efficiency of Trans-Canada Air Lines and would merely be of assistance to the Canadian Pacific Air Lines which itself is a subsidiary of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
We have noted with interest the Wheatcroft report and were pleased that it did not condone any early interference with Trans-Canada Air Lines. With regard to its stated attitude toward T.C.A. in the past we hope the Conservative party will change and will maintain Trans-Canada Air Lines intact in the form in which it now exists, will allow the air line to expand and will turn thumbs down on the proposition that transcontinental flights should be turned over to private companies.
The annual report of Trans-Canada Air Lines in our view is a solid indication of the efficient service of this company. The fact that it has been able to continue to expand at a very rapid rate and acquire the most modern planes and equipment and increase its service and at the same time reduce passenger rates is a worth-while and welcome respite from the kind of action we usually see these days by private corporations. In scarcely any other service can one find a substantial reduction in prices in 1957. I should like the minister to give us a more comprehensive statement than that he has given thus far as to what the policy of the government is going to be with regard to Trans-Canada Air Line services. I hope he will tell the committee the government has no desire to provide so-called competition -and I do not think it is really competition at all-to Trans-Canada Air Line services.
The Wheatcroft report pointed out that not only does Trans-Canada Air Lines provide highly efficient service but to a degree the provision of service by Trans-Canada Air Lines in areas where passenger traffic is not particularly great is in effect a subsidy for the people in that area. As a person coming from the prairies I am naturally interested in having as good service as possible for that region and I realize if we had to depend upon competitive service only without the operation of a public company like Trans-Canada Air Lines which considers the welfare of the general public we might have much less service and service of a considerably poorer quality than we now have.
I wish to associate myself with the hon. member for Laurier and with the Minister of Transport in the tribute they paid to our friend, Right Hon. C. D. Howe. I do not believe there is any one sitting in this committee today who has clashed with Mr. Howe more often than I have. If I have been able to acquire some knowledge of the procedures

of this house and some knowledge of the activities of the Department of Trade and Commerce and in particular some knowledge of the grain marketing business, I can thank Mr. Howe for a good part of it because whenever I asked him a question on orders of the day, even as a new member, he treated me with courtesy and always gave me a full and frank answer. One thing I always liked about C. D. Howe was that he was a good, hard and tough debater. He did not give any quarter and he did not ask any quarter but at the end of a debate one always parted from him on excellent terms.
C. D. Howe is a big businessman. He has acquired much power and authority in the Canadian business world. He has many good qualities but as is the case with every hon. member of this committee he occasionally displayed certain human weaknesses. One quality of his character which I always admired and considered good was that he constantly protected the people within his department and defended the operations of organizations within the purview of his department. When C. D. Howe was the minister in charge of Trans-Canada Air Lines, Polymer Corporation or any other project coming under his department's jurisdiction one could be reasonably assured that the operation would be efficient based in the public interest and would expand.
He was a great miner for talent for the public service.

I believe that is true. I do not think any one could say that in his philosophical make-up C. D. Howe had any particular love for public enterprise and he was probably as anti-socialist as anybody who sat on the treasury benches. But he was a pragmatist and when he saw that public ownership would do a much better job than private ownership in a particular field, in spite of his basic belief he did not hesitate to promote public ownership.
I believe that Trans-Canada Air Lines is one of the best air line services in the world and it has provided excellent service to the Canadian nation without profit. If Canada is going to compete with foreign air lines in providing air services in days that lie ahead we will be more apt to compete in an efficient way and keep abreast of technological improvements if we maintain this publicly owned corporation and refuse to turn it over to private hands. Canada in competition with the air lines of the world should tell the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, the United States and other nations that we have a publicly owned corporation that has the backing of the Canadian government and the
Supply-Transport
Canadian people and that we intend to compete efficiently with all comers. I am hopeful that the Minister of Transport will tell the committee there is no intention on the part of his department to turn Trans-Canada Air Lines over to a private company and I ask him that question.

Mr. Chairman, I am not quite sure what the hon. member has asked. Is he implying that this government is intending to hand over Trans-Canada Air Lines to some private company or is he suggesting that if the air transport board should decide some measure of competition would be beneficial the government should simply refuse to accept the decision of the air transport board?

Mr. Chairman, in answer to the last part of the minister's question I will say yes. The fact that we have established a certain board does not mean that board is paramount to parliament. The board is not paramount to parliament. In recent months the board of transport commissioners allowed an increase in freight rates. The governor in council, by its authority under the law, refused to allow the increase to go into effect. I am asking the minister whether the government-never mind the air transport board -has a policy of maintaining the T.C.A.'s present position on the trans-Canada air lines runs, or whether it is prepared, in the words of the minister, to allow competition in this service?

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member knows and as all hon. members know, the air transport board was established to examine applications brought before it by various air lines in Canada. That is being done at the present time in the case of an application for a trans-continental route. Two air lines have applied for the right to operate on that route as well as the T.C.A. In accordance with the terms of reference under which the air transport board operates, those applications will be heard and the recommendation of the air transport board will be transmitted to the government and the government will examine that recommendation. That is the course we propose to follow.

From my point of view the minister's answer is entirely unsatisfactory. Of course, what the government does in the future can only be determined by events. After the government receives the recommendation from the air transport board, if it should acquiesce in allowing so-called competition which will do nothing but hurt the services in this field the government will be doing a disservice to the people of

Supply-Transport
this country. I am hopeful that in the days that lie ahead the minister will support Trans-Canada Air Lines as it now exists, with the rights it now has, and will maintain an expanding Trans-Canada Air Lines and oppose any diminution of Trans-Canada Air Lines rights and will refuse to allow so-called competition. In the tribute that the hon. member for Laurier has paid to Trans-Canada Air Lines there is implicit in his remarks, though he may not agree, that in the light of its history Trans-Canada Air Lines should be given a full and unimpeded opportunity to continue to improve its now excellent service.

Item agreed to.
Telecommunications division-
452.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment, $11,385,000.

I tried to find some details on page 571 but I could not find any. I am not going to delay the committee, but I would ask the minister whether he would not follow the pattern established by the Department of Public Works and on the last pages of the estimates book give details of the projects that are mentioned in this item so that we would have some idea of the projects in the different provinces for which he is asking money.
I can give the information on the main items but I emphasize-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He wants the minister to do it in the future.

I am not asking for it this year but in future years. Details of the vessels that are to be built are given for this year, but with respect to this item for $11,385,000, I am asking the minister whether in future years we could not have details of the different projects that are included in the item so that we would have information on the projects, as we have been doing in public works.

We will give every possible consideration to doing that. The only difficulty is, it would be a tremendous volume of details but we shall give every consideration to the possibility of doing what the hon. member requests.
I am not asking for all the small projects but just for projects over $100,000.

Item agreed to.
Radio Act and regulations-
453.	Administration, operation and maintenance, including contributions as Canada's share of the costs of various international radio, telegraph and telephone organizations, as detailed in the estimates, $2,359,295.

The other day a question was asked about the opportunity to introduce

United States television programs by the introduction of a cable into Canada. I do not think the minister has replied to that question yet but I, of course, am interested because the location in question in Canada was Fort Frances. It was indicated that a United States firm felt that, without insisting on approval from the department, it could bring in to Fort Frances a program which in turn would be paid for by installation charges paid by the United States company. Another common practice in some communities that cannot get good reception is to pay a monthly rental fee for the service. I heartily approve of this in this particular location because I have some experience with the long delay in getting the C.B.C. sound radio programs in that area. They are 150 miles from the microwave television network and I surmise it might be rather late in the program of the C.B.C. to provide them with service. I think this comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport and I wondered whether the minister could tell us that his department has been dealing sympathetically with the application of International Television Cable Corporation to allow residents of Fort Frances who have subscribed a certain amount of capital for this service and who feel keenly that they are getting television reception from nowhere, to take advantage of it. Is the minister aware of this situation?
Mr. Chairman, we have just heard of this matter informally. The government has no control over a cable of this kind.

The minister asserts that if a company crosses an international river by means of renting a telephone company's lines and introduces programs that it will be possible to recable it on the Canadian side?
I am adviced by my officials that if they wish to bring in this cable they can do so.

Mr. Chairman, this item covers the administration of the Radio Act and regulations. Very briefly I wish to mention four matters which I have been asked to raise on the floor of the house by various organizations and persons in my constituency.
No doubt the minister is aware of the fact that in Kootenay West we have had great difficulties with respect to radio interference occasioned by power lines. The matter has been taken up repeatedly and the minister's officials have visited the district to try to locate the causes and advise the local people how best to overcome it. They appreciate that but I do suggest that the department do everything possible to continue to assist those

people who at the present time are almost denied radio reception completely because of interference from power lines. However, I do suggest that this problem will not be corrected until we have the necessary low-power relay stations.

If the hon member is going to ask all four questions, perhaps I can deal with each one as it comes up. In answer to that question, Mr. Chairman, we are working with the power company in this regard. The difficulty so far is that the signals are very weak indeed. We are continuing to work with them and will do everything we can to be of assistance.

I thank the minister for his reply, and I was coming to that point. I think the signals are so weak the only solution will be the erection of two or three of these low power relay stations. I hope the minister uses his influence with the Minister of National Revenue, and together they will soon have these stations erected.
The other matter to which I wish to refer was piped-in television. I want to explain to the minister that I am not mechanically minded. My mechanical ability ceases with the lawnmower and wheelbarrow. We have piped-in television around the Nelson and Trail areas through coaxial cable service and a reflector on the mountain top. There has been a great deal of complaint about the rates and fees charged when there is a change of occupancy in a house, and things of that sort. I have taken this matter up with the department, and I understand the department issues a licence but has no control over the fees and charges. I have taken it up with the public utilities commission in British Columbia, and they say they accept no responsibility in that respect. Apparently, therefore, the administration of this business lives in a vacuum. I ask the minister if it would not be possible for the officials of his department to take the matter up with the public utilities commission so there is some regulation with respect to fees, charges and other costs exacted by these companies.
My suggestion is that if these people believe these charges are excessive, this would be a matter to take up with the new regulatory board which is in the process of being established.

I thank the minister for that answer. This is like a cricket match, one wicket at a time.
The other matter I should like to mention relates to community television. I have one or two groups in my constituency who have a co-operative arrangement for the use of some sort of reflector on the mountain top 57071-3-276
Supply-Transport
reflecting signals for television, without cables, to certain vital areas in the district. I understand they have been refused the right to instal this system as there is some distinction in law between the use of the air in that way and bringing signals in by coaxial cable. Would the minister inform me why these people are refused the right to instal their own television system when they are unable to obtain any other, and the distinction between this form of television and the one I previously spoke about which is piped-in?

This operation would be completely dependent upon United States programs, so we considered that it would be advisable to hold this matter up and let it be considered by the new board. This is quite an important matter.
Did the minister say that would be referred to the new board?
Our suggestion is the applicants should refer this matter to the new board as soon as it is appointed.

I have one other matter, and then I shall subside for a few minutes. I have had it brought to my attention, Mr. Chairman, and been asked to obtain information as to why the government does not demand commercial operator's standing for station engineers the same as is required under the federal communications act in the United States. I understand our present act allows anyone to operate the physical equipment at a transmitter site and also automatically-operated equipment under the juke box principle, and according to my information this negates the need for any Canadian studying or taking exams in the field of radio broadcasting. I have been asked to inquire of the minister to see if the act could be amended to require licensed personnel as the operators of radio stations?

The technical qualifications of such engineers have to meet the standards set by the department, so in effect what the hon. member believes is not so. We do not allow engineers to operate these stations unless they come up to our technical standards.

May I revert to my former question, and ask whether another form of T.V. service might be provided at a border town? I take it that the minister's department, under the Radio Act, would have control of an organization that picked up a United States broadcast and then relayed it within Canada, but that if a United States company simply provided their service by cable they are exempt from regulation?

Supply-Transport
Yes, Mr. Chairman, that is correct.

Item agreed to.
Telegraph and telephone service-
455. Administration, operation and maintenance, $277,802.
I have one or two questions to ask on this item. Does the Department of Transport operate any telegraph or telephone services within Canada, and if so how many?
There is the Magdalen islands service, the service in Cape Breton and a small service in New Brunswick.
May I ask the minister, are these land lines or are some of them wireless systems?
They are chiefly land lines, Mr. Chairman, but there are some radio links.

I have one more question, and I do not expect the minister to answer this question now. I wonder if, when it is convenient for him to do so, he would give me the population in the areas served by these systems?
Yes, we shall be glad to convey that information to the hon. member.

Item agreed to.
Meteorological division-
457. Administration, operation and maintenance, including grants as detailed in the estimates, $10,708,161.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is one word here which I cannot resist saying because, at times, there is some criticism about the fact that headquarters buildings are removed from Ottawa and given to other cities. I have reference to the printing bureau, which has gone to Hull; to the national film board, which has gone to Montreal; and the seaway headquarters which are alleged to go to Cornwall. I want to say here that, perhaps unknown to the house, the meteorological service of the Department of Transport have their headquarters in the city of Toronto. This is a decision that was taken earlier, and I know when I was holding the position which my hon. friend holds there was a difference of opinion between certain officers of the department and I had to take a decision at one time as to whether the headquarters would be brought back to Ottawa or remain in Toronto. In order that there may be no doubt about the view of the present officers, I can say that those who discussed the recommendation with me are no longer with the department. They have retired.
I did have to seek advice as to what was the best thing to do under the circumstances. I sought the advice of Dr. Andrew Thompson, who is director of the meteorological services.

Of course, he was strongly of the opinion that this service should remain in the city of Toronto. I remember one evening getting a telephone call from the president of the University of Toronto, who is now the Secretary of State for External Affairs, giving strong reasons why, because of the association of the University of Toronto with meteorologists, it was so important that that service be maintained in the city of Toronto. I need hardly tell the house that the decision was taken to leave the headquarters where they are.
My only reason in rising at this time is to say that sometimes it is in the national interest that headquarters buildings be removed from the city of Ottawa and established elsewhere.

I should like to ask the minister if he could give the committee a report on the meteorological stations in the Arctic. How many of such stations are under the sole control of Canada; how many are under joint control; and how many, if any, are by agreement under the control of the United States? Can he tell the committee what progress is being made to ensure that Canada eventually will be able to take full responsibility for this important work in the Canadian Arctic?
In answer to the hon. gentleman's question may I say this. There are five Canadian stations, five joint stations and no United States stations. We have been increasing our component every year.
Can the minister give some idea as to the respective participation of Canadians and Americans in those five joint stations?
We have in each case the officer in charge. We provide 50 per cent of the supplies. We undertake the supply work. We have the majority of the operators in each of the stations.
The minister anticipates that, as Canadian technicians are trained and made available, it will not be very long before we have complete responsibility for the maintenance of those five stations?
Our primary responsibility is to have the new stations on a 100 per cent Canadian basis before we start taking over the joint bases.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is just one matter here that comes to my attention. It has to do with

the statement that the minister made in the house earlier, namely that it would be in the public interest that licences for air services using only the small type of aircraft be granted freely on request. The minister will recall that I asked him a number of questions on that matter because I had received representations from smaller air carriers protesting against that decision. I want to bring it to his attention now, not in order to delay the committee but to point up some of the difficulties that arise. The decision that was taken and announced by the minister is, in my opinion, one which is not in the general interest of these carriers because it opens up the charter aircraft field to wide-open competition. I have grave doubts about the matter lest it bring about bad results which will affect these companies that are operating under difficult circumstances in wide areas of the country at far away points. It strikes me that they will be seriously affected by this decision.
I will go so far as to say this. The minister stated earlier that there should be wide-open competition and that, because of the Wheatcroft report, there had to be a change in policy. It may very well be that it was decided to make that free and wide-open competition in this restricted field; and it may well be that, in order to carry out in part at least the statement or the promise made by the minister earlier, this was being done.
I should like to bring to his attention the fact that many of the air carriers in the class "C" category are greatly disturbed about this decision. They have been established at great sacrifice to themselves and they will be materially and unfavourably affected if this policy is allowed to be carried out. All I want to do is to bring the matter to the attention of the minister and to ask him if he will not reconsider it. I ask him if he will not bring the matter to the attention of his officers, particularly the air transport board, so that they might give consideration to the representations which I am sure these small carriers will want to make to the board, and which I am sure they have already brought to the attention of the minister. Without saying more, I will resume my seat in the hope that the minister will give consideration to what I have said.

On vote 459 which I think comes under the administration of the controller, although my remarks might be equally applicable under vote 460, I just want to raise one or two matters very briefly. When I was the parliamentary assistant to the then minister of transport, the hon. member for Laurier, I had the honour of opening a modest expansion to the Winnipeg 57071-3-2764
Supply-Transport
airport. At that time I said frankly on behalf of the department that this extension was recognized as being merely a temporary expedient. Since then there has been an addition. But on the other hand, the minister's predecessor wrote me in 1956, prior to the change of administration, that he had every expectation that construction of a new terminal building for Winnipeg would commence in 1957. I am wondering whether the minister would tell us something about progress in this respect.
I have another item; and I must say that generally I receive from the Minister of Transport the utmost consideration. I am only going to draw his attention to a little incident that is not going to affect our personal relations very much. I want to point out to him that I made a written inquiry about new construction on the Kenora airport on April 25. While his letter to me was dated June 6 in reply, indicating that it was expected that they would soon obtain a contractor for the work at the Kenora airport, it just so happened that the defeated Conservative candidate in the district was able to make an announcement about this matter two or three days prior to the receipt by me of the letter from the minister. I do not think that is typical of the minister. I am sure it was just an oversight that the letter did not, in the usual channels through the mail, reach me as it should. I am sure the minister would not want that to happen as a regular practice. He will recognize from the dates I gave that I had shown a great interest in this matter long before a reply was possible. Then for some reason or another I did not receive the letter dated June 6 until after the announcement had been made in the Kenora papers by someone else. However, I must give him the full benefit of any doubt; in fact, I really have no doubt. From my own experience I know that sometimes mail presented to me by a secretary is typed for a certain date, and I do not necessarily change the date if I have not had the opportunity on that particular day to sign the letter. I am sure it was not deliberate. However, I am just hoping that the minister will try to avoid that type of thing in the future.
I wish to assure the hon. member that was not intentional.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is just one question I wish to ask. It has to do with the Dorval airport. As the minister knows, the air terminal was envisaged some years ago and there was then designed a plan for this international airport. There are three questions that come to my mind. The first is this. What was the original estimate? What was the intermediate estimate? By that, I mean the one that was made by the immediate predecessor of the minister. Finally, what is the estimate today, in 1958. Then I should like to know from the minister, if he will be kind enough to tell me, why it was necessary to revise these estimates. I take it that it was because of the fact that, during the planning of this important air terminal there were changes in design brought about by the jet era. Strips must be longer and stronger. Where a strip of 4,000 feet or 5,000 feet sufficed at one time, now it is necessary to have strips two or more miles in length.
Four miles?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes; there is a strip several miles in length out here at Uplands airport which is in operation at the moment. Because of the new instruments and so forth it also becomes necessary to amend the plans and specifications. I wonder, therefore, if I could not get an answer in respect to those questions.
There is another question having to do with air conditioning, and I do not want to repeat what has been said earlier. I know the reasons why at the outset it was decided against air conditioning. These were because it was not the policy of the government to put air conditioning in their buildings because it would have brought about a serious delay and would have increased the cost, but I think that in view of the developments in the aviation field a complete change has been brought about with respect to this aspect of the question. There are a number of alternatives which have entered the picture, more particularly the strong recommendation by the international civil aviation organization which strongly favours the air conditioning of new terminal buildings. I therefore hope it will be found possible to make a complete study of this matter and to come up with a recommendation which would favour air conditioning. I also hope the minister will be able to answer my earlier questions.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I will be very glad to do so.

First, with regard to Dorval airport, various cost estimates were made at various stages, although a complete cost estimate was not possible until 1957 because final plans and specifications for the building itself were not completed until that time. Earlier estimates varied from $10 million, when the plans were in the early stage of preparation, to $12.5 million in 1956 and, last year, to $15 million, as the plans and specifications were completed. These amounts were for the terminal building only and not for the ramp area and aero quays and fingers connected with the ramp area. The cost of the fingers and the aero quays is estimated to be about $2 million and if air conditioning is added to the public waiting room, this could run to another $500,000 which, when added to the cost of the main building itself, would give a total of around $17.5 million. It has been necessary because of changing conditions in aviation to modify the plans on more than one occasion. The ability to do this has indeed been an advantage in providing for a more modern terminal since that time and if the plans had been made inflexible in the first instance they could not have kept abreast of the changing requirements of the air lines and indeed the building might have been obsolete in some regards when completed.
The interior layout plans were adjusted on several occasions as the result of discussion with the air lines and with customs and immigration, whose requirements continued to evolve throughout the period. The most difficult issue and one which has only recently been settled related to the fingers and aero quays layout for the movement of passengers to the aircraft.
With regard to the matter of air conditioning, I quite agree with the hon. member for Laurier and with other members who have spoken. In fact a number of the members from the Montreal area have spoken to me about this matter outside of the house and I and my department agree that air conditioning is very desirable if it can be put in without serious delay. During the past week we have been carrying on an intensive study and we shall continue to do so to see if this can be done. As I indicated yesterday, I hope to be able to make an announcement on this matter very shortly.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder if I might follow that up with one or two questions. I believe the various estimates mentioned by the minister were $10 million to $12.5 million, then $15 million and lastly $17.5 million. I take it that these various estimates were made necessary because of a change in the design and plans required by the circumstances which existed from time to time?

That is partly true, Mr. Chairman, and as my officials have advised me, we knew more about the costs of materials and other factors going into the layout as the plans were developed and it therefore became easier to arrive at a more definite figure.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And the first estimate of $10 million to $12.5 million did not include the fingers which the minister mentioned and the other item which escapes me?
The fingers and the aero quays and the possible air conditioning.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: One last question-I understand that this building has been divided into a number of contracts.
That is correct.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There was a contract for the steel, there was one for the foundation and another for the frame of the building. Could the minister tell the house how many contracts have been awarded for this building?
I am advised the number is five.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Could the minister give the breakdown of those five contracts?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. I am advised that first of all there was a contract for excavation and foundation, second, for steel structure, third, for the curtain walls, fourth, for the stone work and fifth, the general completion.

I want to be sure I understand what the minister has said. Is it a fact, then, that in 1956, which I believe was the date he gave, the estimate for this airport building was $12.5 million and then in 1957 it was raised for reasons which the minister mentioned to $15 million, and that if you add the $2 million for what are called aero quays and fingers and the $500,000 for air conditioning, you get a figure of $17.5 million- is that correct?
That is correct.
May I ask the minister who were the lowest bidders in each case and was the contract given to the lowest bidder?

In each case I am advised the contract was awarded to the lowest bidder. It would take some time to give the names and the amounts, but that information could be made available later on if the hon. member desires it.
I will be satisfied if the minister will let me have the names later on.

Would the minister make comment now about the plan for a permanent terminal at Winnipeg? I imagine the minister
Supply-Transport
is very much like his colleague, the Minister of Public Works, who said-although I believe facetiously-that attention would be given to the requests of hon. members in just about inverse proportion to the amount of time they took at this stage when ministers want to pass their estimates. Therefore, I do not want to elaborate on the matter of the development of a public service airport at Atikokan and at Fort Frances. My constituents, however, would feel that I was remiss if I did not at this stage of the debate draw these matters to the attention of the committee of supply for it is of great concern to them.
Thirdly, a public air service between Winnipeg and the lakehead, something which has been lacking for a great many years, was inaugurated when the minister granted a licence for it but has at the moment bogged down because of a lack of adequate airport facilities. The minister does not need to reply to that. He has invited me to speak to his deputy minister and I have had preliminary discussions with him. But has the minister approved anything with respect to the Winnipeg development?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, we have been working with the air lines for the past nine months to try to arrive at satisfactory plans for what we intend to be a first class building. We have worked our way through four different sets of plans to date, and we hope that we are working now on the final set of plans. As soon as this matter is decided, we will be able to go ahead with the construction.

On this matter I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. I understand that the Department of National Defence or T.C.A. are erecting a terminal at Bagotville airport. I should like to know if this means that the department has completely abandoned the idea of establishing a civil airport within the boundaries of the counties of Chicoutimi and Lapointe. I hope the minister has not given up this idea, because this will help me to keep even more pleasant memories of my association with his department.

Bagotville is in the long term plans of the department. At the present time we are moving the civil terminal from its present location to a new location. I am advised by my officials that we are planning a new airfield in the long run but that, as I have said, is a matter of long term planning.

I want to bring up a matter- I think this is the right item-and I wish to do so in no critical sense because I have nothing to criticize. However, I want to impress on the minister, though perhaps he does

Supply-Transport
not need it, the importance of an airfield or an airstrip at least on the north shore of Georgian bay between Sudbury and the Sault to serve what is perhaps the most important industrial development in Canada, that is the Blind River-EUiot Lake uranium development. The population of this Elliot Lake north shore area has grown in a few years from almost nothing to between 25,000 and 30,000. It is the centre of a large investment and of high uranium production. In these circumstances, air travel and air transport are becoming increasingly important. I know that the minister's department is looking into this matter and I know that his officials are co-operating with the local authorities there, but I would venture to emphasize the importance of air transport for this development.
We are examining possible sites in the area, but it is somewhat difficult to find a site which is suitable. However, we are making progress.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

Thank you. May I ask a
question with reference to the airport at Three Rivers? I understand that there is a question of constructing an airport at Three Rivers which would cost in the neighbourhood of $5 million. Is that correct and, if so, may I ask how that airport will be built?
The estimated cost is between $3 million and $5 million. The city provides the site and operates the field and we build the airport.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What is the present position of the negotiations between the department and the city of Three Rivers with respect to the establishment of this airport?
They have agreed to this plan. We expect to award the contract this winter and a survey is going on at the present time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I ask one last question about the airport at Cornwall? The minister knows this has been under discussion for a long time. It was even included as an item in the estimates on one, if not, on two occasions, and that, I think, was found necessary because of the fact that this community is in the centre of the seaway operation and it was felt that it would be a desirable location.
Since then I have seen something which has interested me very much and upon which I must commend the minister. It is that the department intends to establish an airport at Brockville. I commend the minister on this, if it is the case, because I think it would be an excellent idea if there was a milk run between Montreal and Toronto along the St. Lawrence ports to serve places such as Cornwall, Brockville, Kingston and Belleville.

As is the case on the
Winnipeg to the lakehead run.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If it is the intention to proceed in this fashion at Brockville I am sure the minister will want to give Cornwall the consideration it deserves and state that an adequate airport will be established there on the same basis as in the case of Flin Flon and Three Rivers.

Yes, we are willing to enter into the same kind of agreement with Cornwall as with Flin Flon, Three Rivers and other municipalities on the basis of their providing the land and operating the field. We will build it, and we have recently received a request to resurvey a possible site.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Could I make one further suggestion there? It is that perhaps the Cornwall case might be envisaged in a different light in view of the fact that it is now considered the hub of the seaway for both power and navigation. We will certainly give every possible consideration to it.

May I ask the minister to
apply my remarks on a previous item to item 462? Here we have the biggest item in the estimates, amounting to $61 million, and we have no details at all. Yes, Mr. Chairman. We will certainly see what possibly can be done. We will study the matter and make recommendations to the Department of Finance in this regard. As the hon. member knows the Department of Finance would have to agree to anything we may suggest. We will have a go at it.
May I suggest that you follow the pattern established by the Department of Public Works. That is a good pattern.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to hold up the minister. Yesterday the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate made some remarks to which I believe I could simply say "ditto". The minister knows I have had some qualms about the rigidity of the protection of a base under all circumstances within a radius of 25 miles for a

Supply-Transport
class 3 type, I believe it is. On the other hand this seems to be a most radical departure the minister has in mind. It has caused extreme consternation among the smaller air operators in the country. I would imagine that at least 50 per cent of the time spent by the air transport board in the past must have related to applications that are of a type that the minister is going to put in the unregulated field. I believe a second look should be given to this question. I believe there were some rigidities which were not necessary but the complete plunge that is proposed is undesirable in my view. If I am right in thinking that about 50 per cent of the time of the air transport board has been spent in the field of the smaller operators can the minister advise the committee what economies and reduction in staff are likely to result in consequence of this decision. Will the board be reduced? Will the total number of personnel be proportionately reduced as a result of no longer having anything more than what will probably be a routine look at this type of application? As I say, I protest the policy but I wish to know what kind of economy will come as a result of it.
I am advised by my officials that the type of licence referred to covers only 3 per cent of the total traffic in the country.

Perhaps that is so but I am not thinking in terms of mileage or dollar volume. I am thinking about my own correspondence and in terms of the time that would be involved in processing the charter applications. I am wondering to what extent the minister considers that the board under this policy will show a reduction in personnel of civil servants.

Mr. Chairman, the percentage of time spent by the board in the past in working on applications of this type amounted to about 10 per cent. There will be no reduction in personnel in the board. It will simply enable the board to get ahead faster with other types of applications.

Mr. Chairman, I must continue to urge the minister to have another look at this when the session concludes. I know that at the moment he is receiving very strong representations from the aviation industry of this country. They are alarmed and disturbed and I hope a final decision has not been made. I have always felt some modification might be desirable for all classes of licence but I believe the minister has gone too far in the announcement he made to the house this session.

Mr. Chairman, I understand that under this item one can discuss in general terms matters relating to the board of transport commissioners. My remarks will have to do with the railway grade crossing fund.

Go ahead.
(Translation):
I understand those grants were made by the various governments and by the Board of Transport Commissioners for the purpose of giving the general public adequate protection at grade crossings.
Everybody knows that this legislation was enacted some years ago to provide protection at level crossings, because of the increase in highway and railway traffic.
On looking into the matter I have noted that this legislation has been improved from year to year. In fact, there is a government motion on the order paper calling for further improvements.
A case that I would like to deal with more specifically is that of proposed level crossings. I believe that according to the provisions of section 265, paragraph 6 of the act as amended in 1955, a level crossing must have been in use for three years before the Board of Transport Commissioners can make the grant requested.
(Text):
I should like to know if it is the intention of the government to further amend the law so the railway grade crossings to be constructed will benefit from those grants?

Mr. Chairman, there is a bill before the house at the present time which outlines exactly what is going to be done. Any application that has been approved by the board since January 30 of this year, when I made the announcement of an additional amount of money to be set aside for this purpose, will be eligible for the additional grants which will be made available by the legislation which I trust will be passed by parliament on Monday.
Did I understand the minister to say that this will apply to railway crossings that are to be constructed or just to those that are actually recommended?
Anything that comes up from now on during the next three years and any applications that have been agreed to by the board of transport commissioners since January 30 of this year.

Has an agreement been reached between the board of transport commissioners

and the provincial government of Newfoundland with respect to the overpass between the trans-Canada highway and Isle Morte road at the Port aux Basques terminal?
My officials advise me that they do not think that is the case but they will check the files and advise the hon. member next week.
I thank the minister. If agreement has been reached perhaps he can also say what, if any, contribution the federal government is making toward this.
Yes. I will give that information to the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make about a problem in the ridings of Hochelaga and Maisonneuve-Rose-mont under this item. I am going to say a few words in French and then at the end of my remarks I will sum up and ask a few questions.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity of calling the minister's attention to a problem which is peculiar to the ridings of Maisonneuve-Rosemont and Hochelaga. If I include Hochelaga, it is because the hon. member for that riding (Mr. Eudes) has been confined to his home by illness for over a month.
I refer to an old railway line which crosses the ridings of Hochelaga and Maisonneuve up to Montreal East. For about ten years now we have tried to get the C.N.R. authorities to remove this old track and use the one bordering on Montreal harbour. The old track is not only a nuisance, but a hazard to children.
Ten years ago, the Businessmen's Association of Montreal East set up a committee which, after an on-the-spot investigation, made representations to the C.N.R. authorities. Furthermore, the member for Hochelaga and myself met several times with the C.N.R. authorities and tried to make them see that it was time that this track be lifted out, so as to clear up this section of Montreal. To this day we have not been able to convince the authorities that it is a matter of public interest to remove this track and to divert tank car and freight car traffic to the track bordering on Montreal harbour. The C.N.R. management claims this track still serves 25 to 30 industries situated along the track. We doubt this is still the case; at all events, 57071-3-277
Supply-Transport
these trains make several daily journeys across these ridings especially during rush hours, that is, towards 5.30 p.m., with the result that all the north-south and east-west traffic in Montreal East is brought to a standstill for more than five minutes at a time.
Mr. Chairman, this eastern part of Montreal is developing considerably, not only from a residential point of view, but also from a commercial point of view, and the continued use of this track in 1958 is a disgrace for the eastern part of the city, not to mention the resentment and discontent it causes among local residents. There is no reason why Montreal East should be treated differently from Montreal West, and even if the C.N.R. management could show that this track is still a paying proposition, I feel this is no reason for putting their own interest above that of the public, which requires that this time-worn, outdated, obsolete track disappear from our streets.
(Text):
I welcome this opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to ask the minister to take the proper steps and make recommendations to the Canadian National Railways to have the old railway line in the east end of Montreal removed so that the C.N.R. will transport its freight, and so on, along the shoreline of Montreal and not cross the east end of the city. I should like to ask three questions which the minister can take as notice and perhaps give me the information in a few days. If in the meantime the session ends I shall be satisfied if the minister will write me a letter to that effect.
First of all, I would like to know whether the old railway line crossing the east end of Montreal does so under a contract with the city of Montreal? If so, when was this contract signed and when does it terminate? How many industries and industrial plants are served by this old line actually, and what are the names of those industries concerned? What has been the volume of freight on this old line in the past year? What was the volume of freight in a comparative year, let us say 1950 and 1951?
Before taking my seat I would like to say that this old railway line is an eyesore which is impeding the progress of the east end. In a large measure this monstrous railway line which crosses the territory is one of the reasons why the eastern part of Montreal has been slower in its development than the western section. It is not only an ugly sight but a hazard. The minister would certainly

Supply-Transport
render a humanitarian service to our community if he would intercede with the Canadian National Railways and ask them to place the interest of the whole population of the eastern part of Montreal above their financial interests.
I shall be glad to look into these matters and advise the hon. member early next week.

I should like to make a suggestion regarding the problem of the elimination of railway grade crossings. I take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Transport upon having the courage and wisdom to bring forward the most drastic solution to this serious problem of railway grade crossings ever proposed since 1909.
During the last 50 years each succeeding government has had to face this problem with its increasing toll of human life and suffering as well as the detrimental economic losses. However, it is sad to note that even with increased financial help from the federal government from 1909 to 1957 not more than 4,000 level crossings have been protected, of which no more than 1,500 were grade separated, leaving almost 30,000 crossing without any protection.
There is no doubt that with the urban development which has taken place throughout Canada, the increase in the speed of trains, the increase in the number of automobiles, the $63 million which was spent from 1909 to 1958 by the federal government, the provinces, the municipalities and the railway companies, the amount of money spent so far has been only a palliative and not a solution of this problem.
In the city of Montreal itself, the metropolis of Canada, there are about 140 railway crossings, 80 of which have grade separation, 40 are protected only by bells and other systems, and 20 have no protection at all. In addition, there are about 150 sidings crossing city streets which are absolutely unprotected. Statistics prove that in the city of Montreal accidents are 21 times more numerous at level crossings protected by manually or automatically operated gates than at unprotected level crossings. This proves that the only thorough manner of eliminating railway accidents at level crossings is by a long term program of grade separation. However, there has been very little done throughout Canada towards improvement in this direction during the last 50 years.
The proposed measure providing $10 million for grade crossing improvement and elimination is a very constructive one, particularly since one of its main results will be to ease the financial burden on municipalities. This is one of the main reasons that the efforts

made up to date have not met with too much success. In fact, for the next three years, the board of transport commissioners will be empowered, if the proposed measure now before the house is adopted, to increase its share of the cost of these works from 60 per cent to 80 per cent, while the maximum contribution from the board will go up from $300,000 to $500,000. These provisions will most certainly promote the actual separation of rail from road. The government believes it will have this effect because they have announced their intention to make available $10 million annually for the next three years to the railway grade crossing fund. This is almost twice as much as the amount spent by previous governments from 1909 to 1957.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we have had the announcement of a great national development program by the present government, which is being gradually implemented by appropriate measures, which will integrate the human, physical and economical forces of all regions of our great country towards full employment, and which will fully exploit on a long term basis all our potentialities from the Atlantic ocean to the Pacific ocean and even deep into the Arctic regions. The proposed measure tending to reduce useless deaths and suffering and increase the efficiency of our railways and highways certainly is justified in view of the goals set for such an integrated national development program, namely the betterment of the standard of living of every Canadian citizen; the preservation of our human capital and natural resources; the tapping of our numerous undeveloped resources; the broadening of our basic production and the binding of the Canadian economy into a solid, compact unit giving an equal opportunity to every province.
This integral national development program, Mr. Chairman, is bound to provoke the construction of many new highways and the extension of many railway lines as part of a program of public works which is an integral part of this national development program of ours. It would be regrettable if in the implementation of such a program we were still to suffer the plague of level crossings with their useless toll of life and efficiency.
As the present Minister of Finance so aptly said in 1955, it is true that grade separations cost a lot of money but one has to consider also the economic losses and the suffering which occurs every year at level crossings, and which could be avoided. One has to take into consideration also the effects of fast and efficient transportation on the Canadian cost of living. The main obstacle in

the past has been the inability of both railway companies and municipalities to meet the cost of grade separation. Since 1909, the federal government has been forced into showing more and more interest in the national problem of railway grade crossings. Experience has proven that federal aid had to be constantly increased over the years. However, it is to be noted that it was during the economic crisis that most of the grade separations were effected because additional funds were granted to the railway grade crossing fund and even contributions of 100 per cent could be made by the then board of railway commissioners towards these projects.
The present measure provides the most daring effort ever made by any government towards an efficient solution of this problem, and I am entirely in favour of its adoption. The proposal is for a three-year period, probably as a means of testing the effectiveness of the measure with a view towards finding a permanent solution. May I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that during this three-year testing period intensive research be conducted towards finding a way of relieving the municipalities of the financial burden which is worsening their already poor financial situation. If we could integrate these grade separation projects within the national development program we would thus ensure the implementation of an efficient and realistic program of railway grade crossing elimination within a reasonable period of time to the great benefit of our constantly increasing urban population.

I wonder if the minister could advise whether or not there are outstanding before the board of transport commissioners any applications for proposals from the city of Edmonton with respect to overhead or subway crossings of the mainline of the Canadian National which comes into the city of Edmonton? I have one or two remarks to make with respect to shipping on the coast of British Columbia. The report of the royal commission on coastal shipping was made public not too long ago, which cost the taxpayers some $251,000. I am sure residents in other parts of Canada who are affected by coastal trading and shipping generally were interested in this report, but those of us from British Columbia, who are naturally interested in shipping, were hoping for something fairly decent in the way of recommendations by this royal commission. In so far as the British Columbia shipping is concerned, however, it was a complete waste of a quarter of a million dollars. The shipping needs of the people on the coast of British Columbia appear to have been disregarded or forgotten by the gentlemen who composed that royal commission.
For quite a number of years now the attitude of the governments of Canada-and this remark does not apply to any particular government or to any particular minister- with respect to shipping on the coast of British Columbia has been one of negligence. They appear to be fumbling from one year
Supply-Transport
to the next, hoping that not too many difficulties will arise at the start of the year and when the year is at an end they say, "Well, nothing serious happened; we have got through another year, so we don't have to worry too much about it." I am sure the minister will agree with me that this is not too sensible an attitude to have adopted in past years. The needs of the people living in the communities all up and down the coast should no longer be disregarded, nor should the service to them be disregarded in the development of any shipping policy so far as the Canadian government is concerned.
Unfortunately, in the past few years a number of charges have been made that political consideration was the main factor in respect of our coastal shipping. Union Steamships Limited, for instance, is a company which has been operating on the coast of British Columbia for quite a few years, and some years ago it came under the ownership of an hon. member of the other place, a senator who belongs to the Liberal party, When this took place one heard charges laid that the government of the day, which was a Liberal government, was playing political favourites with Union Steamships because the owner of the company was a member of the Liberal party. That, of course, did not help the situation too much; it in fact clouded over the issue and it is unfortunate that these things were said. Then we had another company which was mentioned just a moment ago by the minister, Northland Navigation Company Limited. Until this year this company was actively engaged only in a freight service, but this year it entered into a passenger service on the coast. Charges were made that the Northland Navigation Company had very close connections with our Social Credit government in Victoria, and as a consequence was able to get special favours in respect of the shipment of goods coming under the jurisdiction of that government. That, of course, did not help matters either, but it too tended to cloud over the issue.
Last year we got into a most difficult situation owing to the difference of opinion between one of the companies operating on the coast with respect to the amount of subsidy they needed and for some months during last winter we had no adequate passenger or freight shipping facilities on the coast of my province. The whole program, the whole schedule of routes which had been established over many, many years, and which were adjusted from year to year by the companies concerned, was entirely upset, and many communities were isolated. I got telegrams, letters and phone calls galore, as I am sure did the

Supply-Transport
minister or the officials in his department, as a result of this turmoil in shipping last January.
Unfortunately the picture in so far as the possibility of further charges of political considerations in respect to shipping on the coast of British Columbia is concerned, is a bleak one. I say this because we know that the Northland Navigation Company-and it is certainly within its rights to do this if it wishes and I am not suggesting that these things should not have been done; but I merely raise this to point out that it once again lays the question of shipping on the coast open to charges of political connivance and of favouritism to a particular company- or an officer of that company contributed to the campaign funds of the Conservative party. This is very unfortunate, because the people who suffer are certainly not to any extent the shipping companies and certainly not the federal government, but the hundreds of people living in the many small communities all up and down the coast of the province of British Columbia. There are a number of question marks which we must raise with respect to this particular arrangement which has today been announced by the minister.
We understood, and it was announced by the minister, that when Northland Navigation bought two ships from the C.P.R., the Princess Alberni that used to run along the west coast and the Queen of the North that used to run on the upper coast, those two ships would be operating under the same subvention arrangements that were made with the C.P.R.-the regulations might be changed a little here and there, but nothing too drastic. Northand Navigation entered into an agreement to buy the ships knowing that certain subsidies were in question and that certain routes were involved. Union Steamships and Northland Navigation serve certain parts of the coast and the attitude should have been: no change in the subvention, no substantial change in the routes to be followed; no drastic adjustments in the ports of call. They should be able to operate under the conditions and under the subvention arrangements that existed before they bought the ships from the C.P.R. unless they knew in advance they were going to receive some different consideration.
But we find that Northland Navigation is not going to operate on the same routes as the C.P.R. Whether it is for better or for worse, time will tell, but we find that Northland Navigation is going to change its routing around Vancouver island. Instead of going around the southern end they are to go around the northern end, under subsidy, to compete in effect with a service by another

company to the same areas operating on a non-subsidy basis. We find that part of the northern run the C.P.R. was operating is going to be abandoned. An announcement was made by Northland Navigation a few days ago that the former Queen of the North -I do not know what the name is now; they have changed the name of it-that was operated by the C.P.R. is not now going to call at the Portland canal ports, Fort Simpson, Kincolith, Stewart island and so on. The former Queen of the North is not going to call in at these places. The run to Stewart is going to be abandoned by the ship that was formerly the Queen of the North and added to that is the route into Bella Coola under subsidy competing with the company operating into Bella Coola now without subsidy. We find that Northland Navigation, because it has abandoned the northern route, an additional round trip of about 80 miles, is able to revise its schedule and come into certain ports on the coast about one and a half hours before the Union Steamships are scheduled to call there, they being under subsidy, and Union Steamships not under subsidy.
I understand that under previous subvention arrangements it was difficult for a company receiving a subvention or a subsidy to change its schedule. It had to have prior permission from the Canadian maritime commission, which was most difficult to obtain. Apparently Northland Navigation does not have that difficulty in view of the announcements they make from day to day about changes. It has always been my understanding that the attitude of the governments in the past and the attitude of the Canadian maritime commission is that you should not subsidize one company to compete against another company that is not receiving a subsidy, but that is precisely what is happening in this case.
As I said earlier, the people who will suffer will be the people who live all along these coastal points. From the knowledge we are able to get of the work which will be done in the logging industry on the coast of British Columbia it is likely they will be operating to full capacity with the industry going as far as they can into the winter regardless of the amount of snow because they are short of logs and because markets are picking up to some extent. We find, and I am sure, the government will find this winter, that it will not be necessary to pay a subsidy such as they set out just a moment ago. That is something that should have been taken into consideration in years past. It should have been studied. It should have been looked at. I am sure many people who are interested in this, maybe from a particular point of view, would

like to know-but I do not know-why there was a sudden change in attitude with respect to subsidies that were being paid. I have copies of a couple of telegrams which I would like to read into the record. One is a copy- it did not come out too well, but I believe it is dated August 8-of a telegram to Captain J. A. Macdonell, of Union Steamships Limited, Vancouver, B.C. and it says:
As result various proposals discussed am now authorized advise you submission to treasury board will be made requesting authority pay to you subsidy on basis $150,000 per year prorated tor time served from date of contract to 31 March 1959 calling with vessel Catala at ports listed for Catala route your letter 25 July 1958 with call at Campbell River at your option. Contract will contain recapture clause as outlined to Chestnut. At same time concluding arrangements with Northland Navigation for service similar to former C.P.R. service with Queen of North result of which will be duplication of service at Alert Bay, Namu and Ocean Falls only. No action being taken on your other proposals. Expect Northland to undertake service to four northern ports for which you receive interim subsidy on August 12 so anticipate discontinue interim subsidy accordingly.
That was on August 8 and it was signed by Mr. L. C. Audette, Chairman of the Canadian maritime commission.
On August 11, a Monday, over the week end another wire was sent to Captain J. A. Macdonell of Union Steamships signed by L. C. Audette of the Canadian maritime commission. This said:
Cancel my telegram August 8 concerning your proposals for subsidized steamship service. Urge no action on your part based on my previous telegram.
So during the week end the Canadian maritime commission obviously-and I am quite sure it was this way; certainly not on its own but in consultation with other officers in the department-had decided that certain arrangements were going to be made. Then on Monday the mind of the maritime commission was changed for it and other arrangements were entered into. We wonder why the decision was reversed. We can expect, I am sure, that it was because Northland Navigation Company Limited said: we are able to operate this service at a subsidy or a subvention much lower than that which you have had to pay in years past. The departmental officials undoubtedly looked at this and said: that sounds like a good idea; it is going to cost us less money. Go ahead and do it. And they did this without any investigation of the requirements on the coast other than the cursory one last January when they had to do something. There was no thorough study, no idea of passenger requirements or freight requirements. Why was this decision suddenly taken to reverse completely what had been decided?

That, coupled with the fact, as I mentioned earlier, that political consideration has been dragged into this question of shipping on the coast in years past certainly makes one wonder whether that is still being given consideration.
I certainly do not wish to place on the record any mention of the amount of those contributions or to whom they went, but they were made. It is most unfortunate that after the experience of last winter the government has decided to go ahead with certain subsidies to a specific company for certain routes without giving too much thought about what may happen in years to come. This demonstrates a lack of foresight. When this government took office I sincerely hoped there would be a change of attitude and that there would be someone appointed with a thorough and comprehensive knowledge of shipping and shipping requirements to study completely and thoroughly the problem along the coast of British Columbia and make recommendations and if it were found that subsidies are necessary that person could have decided what they should be, when they should be applied and to what routes they should be applied but so far we have had nothing of that nature.
I repeat again that in my opinion and in the opinion of C.C.F. members as far as transportation is concerned and specifically transportation on the coast of British Columbia there is only one solution. I have heard a number of people who do not belong to the C.C.F. and who certainly are not partial to it agree with the contention that in order to provide adequate service there it must be done through one agency and not through a group of companies, some under subsidy one year and some under subsidy another year depending on who is in office, some having shipments channeled by the government depending on how friendly they are and, all in all, service being a secondary consideration. I am not familiar with the shipping situation in other parts of Canada but unless we can operate shipping on the coast of British Columbia through one agency we are going to continue to experience this turmoil.
I would hope there will be a detailed analysis of the requirements of shipping and transportation on the coast of British Columbia and arising out of that study sensible recommendations made on the basis of the service necessary for those communities that have been disregarded for almost a year.
I hope, just as I am sure the minister hopes, that the announcement he made a moment ago with respect to subventions and the routes they are to cover will not lead us into the same difficulty and confusion we experienced last winter when ports of call were abandoned.

Under this item I believe I can raise the question of tolls charged on the Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges in Montreal. I do so because this problem has been brought to my attention by a number of residents of Montreal and of other residents of the province of Quebec, including Mr. Michel Chartrand, the leader of the C.C.F. party in that province. I am informed that those tolls add to the taxation burden or the burden of doing business in the Montreal area and are a real nuisance to the people who have to pay them. I understand that the Victoria bridge, at any rate, is an old bridge that was paid for many years ago. As far as Jacques Cartier bridge is concerned, its operation is by agreement among the government of Canada, the government of the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal. Under this item, can the minister inform us what consideration has been given to this problem and whether the people of Montreal can look for action from the government which will result in the removal of those tolls in the near future, about which the people of this area feel very strongly?

As a citizen of Montreal, I should like to say a few words on the problem of those two bridges. Is the minister aware of the tremendous increase in traffic which has taken place in the past few years and the difficulties that the people have, especially on week ends, to cross those two bridges in their cars?
If possible, I would like the minister to promise me that one of those week ends after the session is over he will take his car and try to cross one of those bridges on a Sunday.
