The minister at the time answered that the federal government was ready to negotiate a way in which to abolish this whole business of tolls if the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec would undertake to negotiate with the federal government at that time.
Will the minister try to communicate with the province of Quebec and see whether the provincial government is still interested because there are so many things we are stuck with. It looks as if the minister is afraid to communicate with the province of Quebec to see whether the present government of Canada or the government of Quebec is to blame. The people would like to know because the Jacques Cartier bridge and the Victoria bridge are an obstacle to the movement of traffic. Montreal is an island. We have over a million people on that island. Like the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, I suggest that the minister take a drive down there on a week end. If he lived in Montreal I am sure the minister would never use his car on Saturday or Sunday. This is so important that my colleague might want to make another province of the city of Montreal. I do not suggest that he is absolutely wrong. I suggest that the minister communicate with the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal to see whether a means can be found to get rid of tolls because they are obsolete. It is time that we organized Montreal as well as the rest of the country.

Mr. Chairman, I have been asked to bring some figures to the attention of this committee, but first may I say that yesterday the hon. member for Halifax placed figures on the record which showed the very serious disproportion of trade of Canadian produce leaving this country through United States ports rather than Canadian ports. I wish to associate myself in every respect with the remarks he made at that time. Perhaps I should commend him upon the fine research work he did in this regard. This subject has been mentioned on previous occasions in this house, but the hon. member has come up with a very fine bit of work which calls attention to this problem in a very pertinent way. I hope that in later sessions we will have the opportunity of going into this problem in greater detail.
Referring particularly to the port of Saint John, which is my main consideration here today, I want to say at the outset that we are very optimistic about our future. Our industrial expansion in the city has been commendable. We appreciate the new facilities that the Department of Transport is planning. There is a new marine agency wharf, and I understand that plans for a long wharf will be produced shortly. It might be in order also to mention the leadership of the minister in negotiations which are nearly completed with regard to a new oil refinery that will be established there, and the part that the national harbours board played.
However, keeping in mind that optimism, we are a bit worried about the future, particularly in so far as the St. Lawrence seaway is concerned and its impact on the shipping and freight of this nation. We are keeping our eyes open in that regard. Incidentally, I have here, Mr. Chairman, figures which perhaps are not as widely circulated as the tonnage figures issued by the national harbours board. The tonnage figures, of course, do not give the complete story of the actual work a community receives from the movement of freight in and out of that particular port. The figures that are now available, I

think, point up some trend that could be serious for both Halifax and Saint John.
The international longshoremen's association and the shipping federation of Canada keep a record in Montreal, which is audited by Clarkson, Gordon and Company-I have them here and they go back to 1954-which shows the amount of hours and the amount of pay that longshoremen alone received. This record does not refer to any other workers in a port, only the longshoremen. This record is maintained in connection with their various social benefits and particularly in connection with the new retirement plan. I will not put the entire figures on the record today, Mr. Chairman. As I say, they do not necessarily prove anything at this stage, but I should like to compare the eight-month period ending July, 1958, with that same period ending July, 1957. These records show a loss of manhours in the port of Saint John of 345,024; in Halifax of 310,339; Montreal is down, but only to the extent of 176,305, and Quebec is not greatly affected since the loss in this period is only 31,677.
I merely draw this to the attention of the house because it suggests that Halifax and Saint John are going to have to watch their position very closely in the future, particularly when the seaway is open. This may be the beginning of a trend towards a serious decrease in the manhours which the longshoremen work in these particular ports. I know that the department and the national harbours board are on their toes so far as port business is concerned, but I suggest that we will have to come up with some idea of specialized port traffic, something to take away from the extremely seasonal nature of the work and the dependence we have upon the few short winter months that now exist.

I should like to take this opportunity to bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport a major traffic problem in relation to the harbour of Montreal. When the St. Lawrence seaway is completed the harbour of Montreal will no longer be located in a cul-de-sac, and will have to face intensive competition from other Canadian urban centres. This competition will mean Montreal will have to offer better conditions and facilities in its harbour, especially from the point of view of traffic. An extensive study recently made by a McGill University group has demonstrated this very point. The report has shown the need for renovating the traffic facilities in the harbour area.

If one looks at the access roads to the harbour he will be convinced that they were designed a long time ago for means of transportation other than those presently in use. Furthermore, the harbour of Montreal cannot be dissociated from the rest of the city. There is no doubt that the east-west expressway planned by the city along the waterfront should be integrated with the future development of the harbour. In fact, from McGill street to the Jacques Cartier bridge, such an expressway could very justly be considered as a vital part of the harbour itself. Millions of dollars may be spent on grain facilities and other freight sheds, but all these improvements will be useless unless they are served properly by adequate traffic facilities from the city. Let us point out as an example the loading and unloading of trucks in the middle of Commissioner street, which is certainly the least efficient solution which could be found at the present time to these trucking problems.
In this connection the harbour could gain much needed vital space in its most crowded and active section by co-operating with the city of Montreal in the implementation of its project for the rehabilitation of the old warehouse and wholesale district between Place Royale and Bonsecours church, and the integration of the east-west expressway within that rehabilitation project.
May I point out also that parking accommodation is lacking, although the stevedores alone do park more than 500 cars today in the harbour area. Some thought could be given to the suggestion made by the local unions for using the roofs of sheds for parking accommodation until the time when ground space will become available.

Then, there is one final word, and I do not apologize for stating it at this time; it has to do with the headquarters building at Cornwall. I regret very much that there is misunderstanding in connection with this building. I want to make it quite clear that it was always the intention, in the minds of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, to establish at Cornwall the headquarters building of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. That was decided by the government at the time. If that decision is not carried out, I think an injustice will be done to the citizens who reside in that community. At the time what was envisaged was that there would be brought to Cornwall all of the officers of the St. Lawrence seaway authority save and except the head office group which would remain in Ottawa. Over and above that, the headquarters of the canal services would be moved to Cornwall. There would also be the technical engineers and staff of the international board of control that are to remain in existence for a period of 10 years. This is the group that will supervise the operation of the seaway at the level 238 for the first 10 year period after which it will go up to 242. The resident engineers of that board were to be established there as were the toll collectors. Those who would be responsible for the collection of tolls were to go to that area as well as the administrative officers of the Ontario-St. Lawrence canals, making a group of 250 to 300 people. I was keenly disappointed the other day to hear that only about 125 people are going to occupy this building. I hope that is not the case. I hope the minister will see to it that the decision which was made by the earlier government is carried out. It is true that the minister and this government can change that decision; they have the power to do that. However, if they do it, I think an injustice will be done. There is in Cornwall a building which has not been too costly and which is being operated at little or no cost because the then directors, the members of the St. Lawrence seaway authority had, in my opinion, the good sense to rent the ground floor to the Canadian Bank of Commerce for a period of many years, on a long-term lease. I believe that is the only occasion of which I am aware where a crown agency has done that, although I may be wrong. That decision makes it possible for that building to be maintained without cost to the government of

Supply-Transport
Canada. It therefore seems to me that no vacant space should be left in that building. I appeal to the minister to carry out our decision.
I hesitate again to take up another two minutes but I regret the statement which was made yesterday by the hon. member for Dan-forth when he paid tribute to the decision of the Canadian government to get tough on the question of the St. Lawrence seaway, when he paid tribute to the former administration for their determination to see to it that if there was not to be co-operation with the United States government, Canada would go ahead and build the seaway alone. Having said that, with which I find myself in agreement, he went on to add this paragraph which in my opinion is unfortunate and with which I entirely disagree. I quote from page 4290 of Hansard:
But after that our tough policy was watered down. It became lukewarm and the United States eventually took over and dictated the whole policy as far as the St. Lawrence seaway was concerned.
That statement is absolutely incorrect and inaccurate. The whole policy or a great portion of the policy in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway is being initiated by the federal government. It was dictated by the last government and it is being handled by this government in co-operation with the United States government. What we must not forget is this. The St. Lawrence seaway authority has succeeded with the present administration in following the recommendations made by the former administration that all of the tolls-although much of the traffic is going to be on the United States side-Canadian and United States are going to be collected in Canada by the St. Lawrence seaway authority on behalf of the United States authority and turned over to them. This is certainly not dictation by the United States. Furthermore, two-thirds of the canal is on Canadian territory. Two-thirds of the cost is being paid by Canada. It is a joint enterprise so far as operation is concerned. But as to decisions that were taken, certainly Canada has not become lukewarm in the slightest degree. On the contrary, Canada has respected the rights and obligations of others and I believe that Canada is acting in the way it should act under the circumstances.
I am glad to be able to assure the hon. member for Laurier and other hon. members of the house that work on the St. Lawrence seaway is proceeding on schedule.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the minister say what this vote is for?
This is to buy the land that would be necessary in the event that we decided to build an all-Canadian seaway at some future time.

That gives me the opportunity just to say a word because it bears on the point that has been raised by my hon. friend. As the minister knows, this provision was made in order to make certain that in certain circumstances, whether the United States liked it or not, we would have an all-Canadian seaway. Those who say that we have been dictated to by the United States in the development of this waterway, this power development and navigation development, do not know very much about the diplomatic negotiations that went on leading to this development. Those who say that we should have from the beginning insisted on constructing an all-Canadian seaway do not seem to understand that if that was to be done without any power development going along with it, it would have meant a phenomenal expenditure and perhaps be beyond Canadian means at this time. Once it became a power and navigation development, once that power had to be secured from boundary waters, then both governments were involved and there was no other way of doing it. You cannot have a power development halfway across a stream. As it was agreed to be both a power and a navigation development, it was bound to be an international development unless, as I have just said, we had decided to construct a purely navigational development on the Canadian side; and surely that was impracticable.
But we did at that time-and this item in the estimates confirms it-make it quite clear to the Americans that in certain circumstances we could, once the power and navigation project was completed, build another Canadian channel which would make it an all-Canadian seaway. The United States at that time took strong exception to that suggestion. I attended some meetings which dealt with this matter and the language was extremely frank indeed. We were told that this was at the time contrary to their understanding of the original arrangement. We felt that we were acting only in Canadian interests and were acting fairly in this regard. The result was that this action was taken, and there is a continuation in this particular

item of that action which will make it possible for us in the future to have an allCanadian seaway if and when it is desirable.

I should like to reply to the hon. member for Laurier and the Leader of the Opposition by saying that since I have held this portfolio and in the dealings this government has had through the seaway authority with the authorities of the United States there has been no attempt at all by the United States authorities to dictate in any way to us and there has been nothing but complete co-operation and harmony existing between the seaway authority of Canada and the seaway development corporation of the United States.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I just want to add one word and it is this. This item is just one of three things that were done in order to prepare the way for an all-Canadian seaway in case of the accomplishment of the conditions envisaged in the exchange of notes between Canada and the United States, for which my friend the Leader of the Opposition was responsible at the time, came about. The three things were as follows: (1) The construction of a structure in the dike at Cornwall in order to provide for future 27-foot navigation on the Canadian side; secondly, the dredging of a channel 27 feet in depth on the north side of Cornwall island leading to the structure in the dike; and, thirdly, the expropriation of land on the Canadian side from the dike right down to the present locks. These three things provided for a complete canal on the Canadian side of the line in case the volume of traffic was such in, say, two, three, five or more years, that it would be necessary to duplicate facilities on our side of the line. These three things have now been done, which means that 50 per cent of the work leading up to an all-Canadian seaway has been terminated, so that if at a later date it becomes necessary to expand because of the volume of traffic it will be as easy for us in Canada to duplicate the facilities in the international section as it will be for the United States to do so. The thing to do at that time would be to say to our friends in the United States, "We will duplicate at Cornwall, and since we, in Canada, have built at Iroquois, you in the United States go ahead and duplicate opposite Iroquois. Then we will have a Canadian lock on the Canadian side and you will have an American lock on the United States side, the one to circumvent the Long Sault rapids, the other to circumvent the control dam at Rockway point on the United States side." That, I hope will be accomplished one day.

The Minister of Transport has said that there has always been agreement and great harmony between the Canadians and the United States seaway authorities, and I wonder whether that statement indicates that no representation has been made by this government for lower tolls or for a toll-free St. Lawrence seaway. I am all in favour of harmony and agreement, as far as construction and other aspects of the matter are concerned, but as far as tolls are concerned I think that Canada's interests would best be served by a toll-free seaway. The minister's statement that there has been all this harmony leads me to ask him whether the government has pressed for a toll-free seaway.

Several weeks ago I announced in the house a proposed schedule of tolls to be paid by those who use the seaway which would be examined in both countries. I said at that time that hearings would be started on August 6 in Washington and in Ottawa, at which hearings those who would be using the seaway could put forward their views regarding these proposed tolls. The proposed tolls were agreed to by both the Canadian and United States governments. I do not think I can say anymore.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend the member for Assiniboia who has just spoken, will not feel that I wish to enter into an argument with him when I make the following remarks. I think I should remind the house, however, that in 1951 parliament agreed to the imposition of tolls-there is no doubt about it. It was included not only in United States legislation but also in Canadian legislation that this was not to be a charge upon the taxpayer but was to be payable by those who use the seaway. The hon. member for Assiniboia was a member of the house at that time, and I believe must have voted for it, because my recollection is this was unanimously passed-
That is correct.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
-by all parties in the house. I cannot see how, in view of the circumstances, firstly, the agreement between the United States and Canada and, secondly, the legislation passed in this house, it would be possible to have a toll-free seaway at this time.
That does not cover the question of the Welland canal, which is another matter altogether. Whether or not tolls should be extended to that canal is another question, but I think it did envisage a through toll, that is to say from the head of the lakes to Montreal, passing through the Welland canal. As to whether or not there should be tolls

Supply-Transport
on the Welland canal itself, that is to say, for the local traffic, is another matter on which I am not pronouncing any judgment at the moment. I do feel that I should say, however, in fairness to parliament, that in 1951 this matter was clearly established and clearly approved of. This parliament, of course, can alter that, but the impression that was given by the then government and by myself as president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority was that all of these charges were to be paid by those who would be using the facilities and would not be a charge against the taxpayers.

All the statements made by the hon. member for Laurier as to what has taken place may be correct. We have all had the experience of voting for something of which we were completely in favour in principle but which we would like to see amended in some detail, and if the St. Lawrence seaway project was before the house at this time in precisely the same terms as it was back in 1951 I am sure I would support it now as I did then. However, 1951 was some years ago and every session parliament amends acts to bring them up to date in terms of modern thinking. I am suggesting that as the years go by the direction toward which this matter will go -I hope at any rate this will be so-will be in the direction of reductions in tolls on this vital seaway and not in the direction of increasing them. I think that it is perfectly consistent and proper to voice at this time on behalf of many provincial governments and many organizations the request that the seaway be toll-free and to emphasize particularly that as far as the Welland ship canal is concerned it should be toll-free and should be toll-free without any question.
I wish to say to the hon. member for Laurier that while we agreed in 1951 on the seaway project as it was then contemplated and would today agree to the same project, it is nevertheless quite proper to suggest that certain improvements should be made at this time.

I missed the main item being out of the chamber when it was discussed. I have a few remarks to make on this item, and the minister need have no worry about the clock.
For some years past there has been a concerted effort by both the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. to close railway stations in the province of Saskatchewan. They have been making one application after another to the board of transport commissioners to have railway stations closed and to have the agents removed. As a matter of fact, in the last five years no less than 44 stations in the province of Saskatchewan have been closed. Every community that has a station with an agent providing service is, naturally, most reluctant to see its station closed and to have its agent removed. So in many instances when an application is made to the board of transport commissioners residents of the district sign a petition and send it to the board and to the minister and subsequently a local hearing is held. My experience in connection with these local hearings is that they usually accomplish very little as far as the residents are concerned. I have attended some of these hearings myself. The representative from the board of transport commissioners as well as representatives from the railway company appear at a public meeting in a given community. In my part of the country these officials have very often come out of the city of Regina. They ride to the meeting in the same car-I suppose it is economical to do it that way-and they seem to be very much in agreement about what should be done. The representative of the board of transport commissioners is, ostensibly, a person who is sitting in something of a judicial capacity. He is supposed to give everyone a fair hearing but it seems to me that after having driven in the same car with the representatives of the railway company he gives very little consideration to the case put forward by the local residents.
I suppose station agents to a degree have become a casualty of technological improvements and that it is impossible to maintain the same number of station agents now as in the past. Nevertheless it does seem to me that in the closing of these stations the railway application is too often given far greater consideration than the case presented by the local residents. I have had a considerable

amount of experience with these applications. I am rather discouraged by the attitude taken by the board of transport commissioners and their officials. In the vast majority of cases when an application is made the station is automatically closed. The railway company has a long story to tell to the effect that when the station is closed they will put in a caretaker and a telephone and thus maintain facilities. The caretaker is often the wife of the section foreman and in some cases of which I have knowledge they receive the magnificent sum of $10 a month for taking over some of the services once provided by the station agent. Certainly as far as Saskatchewan is concerned, if the operations of the railway came within Saskatchewan labour legislation Saskatchewan would not allow the C.P.R.-that is the railway with which I have acquaintance and for all I know the C.N.R. may do the same thing-
Just the same.

-to exploit the services of those people by paying such a trivial sum.
I do not like to see stations closed. In many instances I have worked hard to keep them open. Although there are a few exceptions, in the majority of instances my efforts have met with very little success. I would hope that the board of transport commissioners would give greater consideration in future to the wishes of the people in the communities where they desire to close the station and remove the station agent.
As far as Saskatchewan is concerned, apparently the railways are out to close most of the stations. They want to maintain only a few agents here and there and close the vast majority of stations. I do not believe this trend can be entirely arrested and I do not think I would ask the board or the government to go that far but I would hope that in future there would be much more consideration given to the advice of local residents and not a continuation of something that appears to be a cut and dried decision made in advance. In many instances the meetings that are held to consider the application are just a farce and an insult to the intelligence of all the people who participate in them. It does not seem to matter how good your case is. Nothing happens and the station is closed down in due course.
It may be that if a federal election is being held and you create enough opposition concerning it they will delay closing the station until after the election but immediately following the election they go merrily on their way closing stations at the same rate. I hope the minister will put the brakes on the board of transport commissioners in this respect.

speechtext:
On that item I would just like to bring to the attention of the minister, since we are discussing a matter concerning Cornwall, the exchange of correspondence we had arising out of the desirability of establishing port facilities in that area. The minister will remember an application was pending for the establishment of a port authority in Cornwall and the minister replied that the old canal facilities would be turned over to the seaway authority there so that advantage could be taken of them for industrial development at Cornwall. While on the face of it that may appear an answer, I am afraid when it is studied it is not satisfactory. It is not because the old facilities are located on a 14-foot navigation canal that industry will be attracted and the minister knows the moment the seaway is opened all of these 14-foot vessels will become obsolete and the new 27-foot vessels will be in demand for use in the new channel.
The area where the port authority was requested is an area in deep water. The water in that area is anywhere from 25 feet to 40 feet deep so the depth is sufficient. It would be unfortunate if the one were traded off for the other. This is a matter that will eventually have to be decided by the municipal authorities of the city of Cornwall. It is for them to determine what is in their best interests. However, I am merely bringing to the attention of the minister the fact that the alternative is not the answer. There must be there for the future development of the community deep water facilities, namely 27-foot facilities, and the area they have suggested seems the most logical one in which to establish them.

Mr. Chairman, I must confess I have not done enough research on
Supply-Transport
this item, not that I especially feel I should have done so. I think this type of thing has probably gone on for some time but it is not fair to hon. members of the committee of supply because it requires them to do some individual investigation of the statutes without the slightest initimation of what the item is all about. I have no doubt this is traditional but I wonder if the minister would give a little explanation.

I would be very glad to do so, Mr. Chairman. At the present time the department operates a revolving fund of $5 million for the purchase of stores required in the various operating branches of the department. During the past year there has been a considerable expansion of the activities of the air services branch chiefly as a result of the taking over of a number of establishments from the Department of National Defence and also the program for the establishment of surveillance radar equipment at 15 airports across Canada.
There has also been a marked increase in the activities of the marine services branch chiefly in regard to the operations of the dominion steamers and also the establishment of a district marine agency at Fort Smith, Northwest Territories. Consequently, it is considered that there now exists a need to increase the stores revolving fund by a total amount of $1 million to take care of the following increased requirements:	(1) increased stocks of radio spares, chiefly for surveillance radar equipment, $500,000; (2) sub-stores depot for radio spares laboratory at Ottawa, $70,000; (3) estimated additional amount required to take care of increased commodity prices, unforeseen new stock requirements and a working capital equal to one month's stores issue, $180,000; (4) printing and stationery stocks for the meteorological service, Toronto, $250,000, making a total of $1 million.

I thank the minister for his explanation. I merely want to suggest that we have had a great turnover in members of parliament. I had some association with this department and I probably should have recollected this but I did not and no doubt not more than two members of the committee had any knowledge of what this was all about. There was nothing in the estimates in layman's language to indicate what it is. I suggest to those in the treasury board who draft these estimates that this is not a proper attitude to adopt toward hon. members of parliament and particularly in the last stages of the session when it is difficult for hon. members of the committee to go to the statutes and find what the references are.

Mr. Chairman, may I say first that the Postmaster General was listening very carefully to what I was saying even though it was noisy in the house. I was saying that the Postmaster General was not a newcomer because when he was an ordinary member of parliament he had access to the offices of the department to the extent that even the material that was supposed to be confidential between the minister's officials and the minister himself was made available to him.
I want to refer to a statement which was made by the Postmaster General on July 26 when he said, as reported at page 2742 of Hansard.
I find that in my general remarks here I have dealt I think with most of the points raised by the hon. member for St. Denis. Again I want to

emphasize the fact that I do not accept his statement that I claimed the post office was poor or that it offered poor service in previous years. I never said that.
I want to answer that statement. He did not say that word for word. I did not even say that he said that the post office was poor, but he made many statements to that effect. I do not know whether his memory is poor but on July 26 I quoted what he said as follows:
But I criticise in the very strongest terms the Postmaster General for his administration of the department, and1 for many of the ways in which it is administered under his direction.
He was referring to the former postmaster general. He said: "It is administered", not the way it was administered. If I understood him, he wished to tell the committee that he was criticizing the postmaster general alone. I do not know why he says in one sentence that the Post Office Department is second to none and in the next sentence that the postmaster general is no good. He has to choose between the two; he has to choose one or the other. If the Post Office Department is well administered, or if he had nothing to say against the officials and the way in which they did their work, why did he say that the postmaster general was no good? Was it because he was not good-looking, was it because he was not well dressed, or something? I do not understand. He has to choose between the two. He made many statements during the time he sat in opposition. I therefore challenge his statement that he never criticized the department. He talked against the post office saving bank. He criticized the way in which security was carried out in the post office. He even wanted the mounted police to take over so far as thefts were concerned. He even said that the department was slow moving. I do not know whether I have the statement here but on January 20, 1956, the minister said, as reported in Hansard at page 363:
Slow moving as the department is and slow moving as the minister may be, we at least have sufficient time for him to make up his mind and do something about this particular situation.
If that is not criticism I wonder what he meant by criticism. As a matter of fact, every time he criticized the departmental officials or the service the name of the minister was always included. He even went so far as to call the minister of that time a stupid minister. I do not know whether he is trying to imitate the former postmaster general so far as thefts are concerned. I heard him say last week that there were about twice as many burglaries under his administration but the amount of money taken was not as large. So far as stupidity is concerned, I think that

was a stupid sentence. It is not the fault of the postmaster general if the burglary is $12 instead of $1,200.

the result of this Postmaster General's changes in the system.
